method: Eight parallel literature sweeps (the papers cited in Jeff Nippard's exercise-science videos and articles, used only as pointers, plus independent PubMed/PMC searches by muscle region, use case and methodology). Each paper was read from PubMed/PMC or the publisher, findings were paraphrased with exact numbers, and a second agent re-opened every source to confirm, correct or reject each finding. Preprints (and findings whose numbers were read from a preprint of a published paper), animal and cadaver studies and practitioner opinion columns were removed. Exercise names were mapped to free-exercise-db ids, and two independent reviewers then checked each match against the catalog record (movement, implement, and any stance or angle the study varied); only matches both kept remain. Unmapped names keep an empty list.
caveats: muscleActivation is surface EMG amplitude from acute sessions; it is not evidence that an exercise grows or strengthens a muscle.
Hip flexors are recorded under quadriceps and serratus anterior under shoulders, because the catalog has no finer muscle names.
Certainty above low is allowed only for syntheses (meta-analyses, systematic and umbrella reviews, position stands).

gaps.problem: There are 32 muscleActivation findings but no human lat-specific hypertrophy trial. Of the 2 hypertrophy entries, one is a quail stretch-overload study (10.1152/jappl.1993.75.3.1263) and the other is a whole-body DXA fat-free-mass proxy (10.3389/fphys.2017.01105). localEndurance has 1 entry (velocity-loss pull-ups), and its between-group difference was not significant. As a result, no lat exercise can be ranked for growth from non-EMG evidence.

gaps.area: traps: hypertrophy, strength, localEndurance (in practice EMG-only)
gaps.problem: There are 24 muscleActivation entries. The single hypertrophy entry and the single localEndurance entry both come from an NSCA expert-prescription article on the upright row (10.1519/SSC.0b013e31822ec3e3), which contains no trial data. The single strength entry is the pooled weightlifting-movement load in Morris 2022 (10.1007/s40279-021-01627-2), where the traps tag is inferred. So there is no trial-based trap size or strength evidence at all.

There are 17 muscleActivation and 10 posture entries (mostly clinical kyphosis and scapular programmes). The single hypertrophy entry is whole-body DXA. The 2 strength entries are a prone bench pull inside a free-weight vs machine comparison and a tempo-review citation. No rhomboid or mid-trapezius size trial with rows was found. My PubMed searches for rhomboid or middle-trapezius thickness after row training returned nothing, so this may be a real gap in the literature rather than a retrieval miss.

There are 18 muscleActivation findings (side-lying abduction, clamshell and band walk EMG). Hypertrophy has 1 entry, an indirect one: gluteus medius and minimus barely grew after hip thrusts or squats. Strength has 1 entry, a side effect of Copenhagen adduction training. No trial trained hip abduction directly and measured gluteus medius size or strength, so the EMG rankings are the only basis for choosing an abductor exercise.

There are 53 muscleActivation entries. Of the 4 hypertrophy entries, one is an expert argument with no trial (10.1519/SSC.0b013e3182259d05), one is a soccer stabilisation MRI study with no group effect, one is rectus abdominis CSA from a free-weight vs machine trial, and one is whole-body DXA. One of the 3 strength entries is expert advice from the same NSCA article. No trial directly compares abdominal exercises such as the crunch, the roll-out and hanging raises for growth or strength.

Hypertrophy rests on 1 finding (a handgrip muscle-thickness study with no measurement site). Strength has 4 entries, and two of them are grip results pooled from a circuit meta-analysis or a periodised programme. There is no localEndurance or power evidence. Wrist curls, reverse curls and grip work cannot be ranked from outcome data.

Calves have 15 hypertrophy findings but only 1 strength finding (light vs heavy isometric plantarflexion) and no localEndurance evidence. Standing vs seated raises, foot position and ROM are compared only on thickness.

gaps.area: hamstrings: eccentric-strength evidence for the Nordic hamstring exercise, and localEndurance
gaps.problem: The only Nordic training trial is Bourne 2017. The widely cited Nordic dose-response and meta-analytic evidence on eccentric knee-flexor strength (and biceps femoris long head fascicle length) is missing. Hamstring localEndurance has 0 entries.

gaps.area: programming variables: weekly volume (hypertrophy and strength)
gaps.problem: Volume evidence comes only from the 2025 Pelland meta-regression and a SportRxiv preprint (10.51224/SRXIV.537). The foundational primary and meta-analytic volume papers are absent, including the one trained-men RCT showing that volume affected hypertrophy but not strength.

gaps.area: programming variables: frequency, rest interval, failure, load, progression
gaps.problem: Frequency for strength and the updated frequency-hypertrophy meta-analysis are missing. The Schoenfeld 2016 frequency meta-analysis is listed as unreadable yet still contributes a finding. The only primary trial of inter-set rest in trained men is missing, as are the Morton load/hormone trial and the Grgic failure meta-analysis. Lasevicius 2018 appears only as a secondary citation, and the load vs repetition progression trial is also missing. Most of these would yield findings with no muscle tag, so they help the rule engine but not muscle mapping.

gaps.area: biceps/triceps: adding single-joint work to multi-joint programmes
gaps.problem: Whether curls and extensions add anything to presses and pulls is central to exercise selection, and the evidence here conflicts: Gentil 2015 and Mannarino 2021 disagree. The companion RCT that tested adding single-joint exercises is missing.

gaps.area: shoulders: rotator cuff and serratus strength (no vocabulary term)
gaps.problem: Shoulder strength evidence is mostly pressing 1RM. Rotator cuff and serratus anterior appear only as EMG findings (e.g., 10.1111/sae.12010, 10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247), and serratus is force-mapped to shoulders. There is no training evidence for external-rotation strength.

Chest, triceps and shoulders have only 2-3 power findings each. These are either cross-sectional correlations (shot put vs bench 1RM; pectoral volume vs bench-throw power) or a null low-load push-up trial. No training trial of ballistic upper-body work (bench throw, medicine-ball throw) was found. A PubMed search for such training RCTs returned nothing. What exists is acute potentiation evidence, which is not a training adaptation.

Several muscles have no localEndurance evidence: hamstrings, calves, adductors, abductors and forearms. Biceps, lats and traps have 1 entry each, and the traps entry is expert opinion. Many existing localEndurance entries record acute within-session rep counts rather than training adaptations: reps at 10RM after pre-exhaustion (10.1519/1533-4287(2003)017<0411:eopeol>2.0.co;2), reps lost after pre-set stretching (10.1007/s00421-016-3527-3), and external-focus reps (10.1080/1750984X.2012.723728). These should be separated from chronic endurance outcomes.

Every muscle's single cardiorespiratory finding comes from one soccer pre-season trial (multi-joint vs single-joint, 10.3389/fphys.2017.01105). All other cardiorespiratory findings (circuit, HIFT, concurrent-training and older-adult metas) have an empty muscle field. As a result, no exercise-level cardiorespiratory recommendation can be derived.

Several entries are counted as outcomes but are not training evidence. Expert-opinion NSCA articles are tagged hypertrophy, strength or localEndurance (10.1519/SSC.0b013e3182259d05, 10.1519/SSC.0b013e31822ec3e3, 10.1519/SSC.0b013e3182221ec2). An animal study is counted as lat hypertrophy (10.1152/jappl.1993.75.3.1263), and a cadaver moment-arm study is tagged strength for the neck (10.1016/j.jbiomech.2010.09.036). A static MRI position study is tagged posture (8222458). Acute 1RM or 6RM load capacity is tagged strength (10.1519/JSC.0b013e318276b873, 10.1097/JSC.0000000000000232). Cross-sectional correlations are tagged strength (10.1519/JSC.0000000000000306, 10.1080/02640414.2024.2430855). Barbalho 2020 (10.1055/a-1082-1126) carries published data-integrity concerns. A number of 'unreadable' papers (e.g., Zabaleta-Korta 2021, Mannarino 2021, Pedrosa 2022, Kassiano 2023, Varovic 2025, Martinez-Cava 2022, Calatayud 2015, Pinto 2025, Barbalho 2020, Pallares 2020, Robinson 2024 preprint values) still supply findings, which should be flagged as abstract-only or partial. Lopez 2021 values are marked pre-corrigendum and need rechecking against the corrigendum.

Hip flexors (iliopsoas, sartorius) and rectus femoris-as-hip-flexor are mapped to quadriceps in the sit-up and leg-raise EMG findings (e.g., 10.1007/s004210050135, 10.1093/ptj/86.5.656). Serratus anterior is mapped to shoulders. Tibialis anterior and posterior, flexor digitorum longus and peroneus longus are mapped to calves (10.1016/j.ptsp.2017.08.077, 10.1097/00005768-200204000-00019). Tensor fasciae latae is mapped to abductors. As a result, activation counts for quadriceps and calves include muscles that the exercises in question do not target.

contradictions: Lat pulldown bar position: the primary Sperandei 2009 paper (10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181b8d30a; PubMed abstract PMID 19855327 re-checked) found no lat EMG difference between behind-neck, front and V-bar pulldowns. The review 10.3390/jfmk11030315 credits the same study with a front-over-behind concentric lat advantage. The review's secondary claim should not override the primary result.

Pulldown grip width and orientation: Signorile 2002 (10.1519/1533-4287(2002)016<0539:ACEIOM>2.0.CO;2) found a wide front grip beat all other grips for lat EMG. Andersen 2014 (10.1097/JSC.0000000000000232) found no whole-rep grip-width difference, with wide above narrow only eccentrically. Lusk 2010 (10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181ddb0ab) found pronated beat supinated, whereas Lehman 2004 (10.1186/1476-5918-3-4) found no significant wide-pronated vs supinated difference (26.2 vs 22.4 %MVC).

Incline vs flat pressing for the upper pectoral, EMG: Trebs 2010 (10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181ddfae7) found 44 and 56 degrees above flat. Barnett 1995 (10.1519/00124278-199511000-00003) found incline no higher than flat. Rodriguez-Ridao 2020 (10.3390/ijerph17197339) found 0-45 degrees did not differ pairwise, despite its abstract claim. Lauver 2016 (10.1080/17461391.2015.1022605) found differences only in the 26-50% portion of the concentric phase.

Incline vs flat pressing, growth: Chaves (10.70252/FDNB1158) found incline grew only the upper pectoral site more, with mid and lower sites similar. The variation review (10.1519/JSC.0000000000004258) summarises incline as beating flat for pectoralis thickness overall (+55-62% vs +32-43%). Pinto 2025 (10.1519/JSC.0000000000005045) found no region-specific pectoral growth with the pec deck.

Rectus femoris growth from squats: 10.3390/ijerph192316226 found 7 weeks of high-bar squats grew rectus femoris like the other heads. Kubo 2019 (10.1007/s00421-019-04181-y) found rectus femoris volume unchanged after full or half squats. Maeo 2024 (10.1249/MSS.0000000000003957) found only +1.1% (non-significant) after leg press. Zabaleta-Korta 2021 (10.1080/02640414.2021.1929736) found Smith squats grew only central vastus lateralis. The Vigotsky review (10.3389/fphys.2017.00985) cites squat trials showing no rectus femoris growth.

Overhead vs neutral-arm triceps extension: Maeo 2023 (10.1080/17461391.2022.2100279) found overhead grew the long head more (+28.5% vs +19.6%, MRI). Stasinaki 2018 (10.3390/jfmk3020028) found overhead and push-downs did not differ. The single-study summary in 10.1016/j.smhs.2025.03.001 even shows the push-down ahead proximally (14% vs 0%).

Partial vs full ROM for triceps: Goto 2019 (10.1519/JSC.0000000000002051) found a 45-90 degree partial ROM beat full ROM (CSA +48.7% vs +28.2%). Wolf 2025 (10.7717/peerj.18904) found lengthened partials equal to full ROM. The Kassiano 2023 mid-range partial advantage (ES 1.21, 10.1519/JSC.0000000000004415) probably re-counts the same Goto trial, so it is not independent support.

Full vs partial ROM meta-analyses: Pallares 2021 (10.1111/sms.14006) found full ROM gave more lower-limb hypertrophy (ES 0.88). Wolf 2023 (10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.182) found no overall size difference (SMD 0.04). At trial level, Bloomquist 2013 (deep beat shallow, 10.1007/s00421-013-2642-7) conflicts with Kubo 2019 (knee extensors 4.9% vs 4.6%) and with the leg-press depth trial 10.1080/02640414.2025.2481534 (similar gains).

Training frequency for hypertrophy: Schoenfeld 2016 (10.1007/s40279-016-0543-8) found twice weekly beat once weekly with volume equated (ES 0.49 vs 0.30, P=0.002). Pelland 2025 (10.1007/s40279-025-02344-w) found the frequency effect inconsistent and possibly negligible once weekly volume is modelled (0.32% per session, CrI -0.14 to 0.82).

Load and hypertrophy: Fry 2004 (10.2165/00007256-200434100-00004) proposes 80-95% 1RM as optimal, and Campos 2002 (10.1007/s00421-002-0681-6) found no significant fibre growth with 20-28RM. The Schoenfeld 2017 meta-analysis (10.1519/JSC.0000000000002200), Lopez 2021 NMA (10.1249/MSS.0000000000002585), Mitchell 2012 (10.1152/japplphysiol.00307.2012) and Schoenfeld 2015 (10.1519/JSC.0000000000000958) all found similar hypertrophy across loads when sets reach failure.

Do pulling exercises grow the biceps as well as curls? Gentil 2015 (10.5812/asjsm.24057) found lat-pulldown-only matched curl-only for elbow-flexor thickness (+6.10% vs +5.83%). Mannarino 2021 (10.1519/JSC.0000000000003234) found curls doubled row-trained growth (11.06% vs 5.16%, p=0.009).

Squat vs hip thrust for glute growth: Barbalho 2020 (10.1055/a-1082-1126, with data-integrity concerns) found the squat grew glutes more than the hip thrust (+9.4% vs +3.7%). Plotkin 2023 (10.3389/fphys.2023.1279170) found similar MRI growth, slightly favouring the hip thrust. Acute EMG (10.1123/jab.2014-0301) strongly favoured the hip thrust. Maeo 2024 (10.1249/MSS.0000000000003957) found the leg press grew gluteus maximus 15.4%, so a large EMG advantage did not predict the growth ranking.

Squat depth and glute EMG: Caterisano 2002 (10.1519/1533-4287(2002)016<0428:TEOBSD>2.0.CO;2) found the glute share rose with depth (16.9% to 35.4%). The glute review 32132843 cites a load-matched study where partial squats beat full squats, and another with no parallel-vs-full difference. For training, Kubo 2019 favours full depth for glute growth (6.7% vs 2.2%).

Foot position in calf raises: Nunes 2020 (10.1519/JSC.0000000000003674) found toes-out favoured medial and toes-in favoured lateral gastrocnemius growth, and Riemann 2011 EMG (10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181cc22b8) agrees. However, the 45-degree leg-press calf-raise study (10.17784/mtprehabjournal.2017.15.529) found no foot-position effect on any head (P=0.75). Akuzawa (28515978) found medial gastrocnemius activity barely changed with foot position, and toes-in produced no head difference.

Knee angle and calf EMG: 10.1519/JSC.0b013e31824435cf reports soleus about 4% higher and gastrocnemius about 5% lower with the knee bent. 10.1016/s1050-6411(03)00058-0 found no EMG change across knee angles of 60-180 degrees. For training, Kinoshita 2023 (10.3389/fphys.2023.1272106) found seated raises did not grow soleus more than standing raises (2.9% vs 2.1%, p=0.410).

Roll-out and Ab-Slide for rectus abdominis: Escamilla 2006 (10.1093/ptj/86.5.656) and 10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf rank roll-out devices highest for abdominal EMG. Sternlicht 2004 (15085210) found the ABslide gave the lowest upper rectus abdominis EMG (148 vs 213 for the trunk curl), though it used non-normalised EMG.

Static stretching before sets: 10.1007/s00421-016-3527-3 found pre-set stretching blunted vastus lateralis growth (7.4% vs 12.7%). 10.1519/JSC.0000000000003283 found no effect on biceps femoris growth when stretching preceded leg curls. Inter-set stretching boosted vastus lateralis in 10.1519/JSC.0000000000003036 but gave no pectoral or quadriceps benefit in the trials summarised by 10.3389/fspor.2022.1035190.

Training at long muscle lengths: lengthening via joint position favoured longer lengths in three trials, namely seated vs prone leg curl (10.1249/MSS.0000000000002523), overhead triceps (10.1080/17461391.2022.2100279) and reclined leg extension (10.1080/02640414.2024.2444713). Resistance-profile bias with ROM matched showed no effect in any of four muscles (10.51224/SRXIV.660), and cable-curl shoulder position was null (10.3389/fphys.2026.1750722). Yet incline vs preacher curls found region-specific differences (10.1055/a-2517-0509).

Free weights vs machines for strength: Haugen 2023 (10.1249/MSS.0000000000003271) found similar gains, with each group best in its own modality. The meta-analysis 10.1186/s13102-023-00713-4 found free weights better when testing was on free weights, and machines better for upper-body strength tested on each group's own modality (SMD 0.245).

Core training and jumping: the meta-analysis 10.5114/biolsport.2023.123319 reports core training improves vertical jump (SMD 0.69). Prieske 2016 (10.1111/sms.12403) did not report countermovement-jump improvement. Hoshikawa (10.1519/JSC.0b013e31828bed36) found jump gains only within the stabilisation group, with no between-group sprint effect.

Hip thrust and sprinting: Contreras 2017 (10.1519/JSC.0000000000001510) found possibly larger 10-20 m sprint gains than with front squats. The review 31191088 reports that 2 of 4 hip-thrust training studies found no sprint improvement vs control.

Leg curl vs hip hinge for hamstrings: Schoenfeld 2015 (10.1519/JSC.0000000000000598) found the lying leg curl beat the stiff-leg deadlift at distal sites. The deadlift review (10.1371/journal.pone.0229507) reports the same Schoenfeld sample both as favouring the leg curl and as favouring the stiff-leg deadlift for upper hamstrings, and cites McAllister finding the Romanian deadlift above the leg curl for biceps femoris.

Inverted row and lats: the primary Fenwick 2009 finding (10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181942019) shows the inverted row's advantage only on the left latissimus, which was the non-pulling side for the one-arm cable row, with no exercise effect on the right lat. The review 10.3390/jfmk11030315 summarises the inverted row as giving the highest lat EMG outright.

Internal inconsistencies within single sources: in Coratella 2022 (10.3389/fphys.2022.825880) the conclusion denies an anterior-deltoid difference that its results report. Sperandei 2009's abstract and results disagree on eccentric pectoral effects. In Rodriguez-Ridao 2020 the abstract claims a 30-degree advantage that its pairwise tests do not support. Robinson 2024 values come from the preprint, not the published version.

findings.finding: In 24 adults, 10 weeks of once-weekly dynamic variable-resistance cervical extension (8-12 reps to volitional fatigue) raised isometric neck-extension strength at 6 of 8 tested angles in the 14 trainees, while the 10 non-training controls did not change.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed truncated; complete abstract read via Crossref record)
findings.population: 14 trained vs 10 control adults (mean age 23-25 y), 10 wk

exercises.name: dynamic variable resistance cervical extension training

findings.finding: All four 12-week cervical-extension machine groups gained isometric neck-extension strength at every tested angle versus non-training controls (n=19), except the once-weekly dynamic-only group at 0 degrees of flexion. Percentage gains are not given in the abstract.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed; truncated at 250 words, remainder not accessible)
findings.population: 50 men and 28 women (mean age 26-30 y), 12 wk

exercises.name: machine cervical extension training (1 dynamic set, with or without 1 maximal isometric set, 1 or 2 days/week)

findings.finding: Groups training cervical extension twice weekly showed a greater isometric neck-extension strength increase than once-weekly groups over 12 weeks. The accessible (truncated) abstract gives no magnitudes, no p-value for this comparison, and no verdict on adding the maximal isometric set.
findings.population: 50 men and 28 women (mean age 26-30 y), 12 wk

findings.finding: Adding 3x10RM head extension, 3 days/week, grew total neck CSA from 19.5 to 22.0 cm2 (splenius capitis +23.9%, semispinalis capitis +24.0%, semispinalis cervicis +24.9%); the same compound lifts without neck work left neck CSA unchanged (19.6 to 19.7 cm2).
findings.population: 22 active college students (mean 21 y), 12 wk

exercises.name: head extension exercise (3x10RM) plus squat, deadlift, push press, bent row, mid-thigh pull
squat, deadlift, push press, bent row, mid-thigh pull without neck exercise

findings.finding: The head-extension 3x10RM load rose from 17.9 to 23.9 kg only in the group that performed the neck exercise; the compound-lift-only group (17.6 to 17.7 kg) and controls (10.1 to 10.3 kg) did not improve over 12 weeks.
findings.population: 22 active college students (mean 21 y), 12 wk

exercises.name: head extension exercise (3x10RM) plus compound lifts

findings.finding: The compound-lift programme without neck work (3 days/week, 12 weeks) increased quadriceps femoris CSA by 7% on MRI (P<0.05), indicating the programme was an adequate leg stimulus even though it produced no neck hypertrophy.
findings.population: 6 active college students (RES group), 12 wk

exercises.name: squat, deadlift, push press, bent row, mid-thigh pull programme

findings.finding: After 19 weeks of leg press and leg extension (6-12RM to failure, 4-5 sets, 2 days/week), concentric-eccentric training enlarged vastus lateralis Type II fibres 32% and mean fibre area 25%; concentric-only training with matched sets produced no significant Type II growth.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed truncated; complete abstract read via Crossref record)
findings.population: 34 middle-aged men (8 CON/ECC, 8 CON, 10 CON/CON, 8 control), 19 wk

exercises.name: concentric+eccentric leg press and leg extension
concentric-only leg press and leg extension (same number of sets)

findings.finding: Doubling concentric-only sets gave Type II (27%) and mean fibre (20%) growth similar to concentric-eccentric (32%, 25%; within-group significance only), but only concentric-eccentric enlarged Type I fibres (14%) and retained mean fibre hypertrophy after 4 weeks of detraining.
findings.population: 34 middle-aged men (8 CON/ECC, 8 CON, 10 CON/CON, 8 control), 19 wk

exercises.name: concentric+eccentric leg press and leg extension
concentric-only leg press and leg extension with twice as many sets

findings.finding: Adding wrist and forearm exercises (not named in abstract) to a 12-week, 3 days/week periodised programme gave significantly larger gains than the programme alone in every 10RM test: barbell wrist flexion and extension, and dominant and non-dominant supination, pronation, radial and ulnar deviation.
findings.population: 43 male high-school baseball players (mean 15.3 y), 12 wk

exercises.name: periodised resistance programme plus wrist and forearm exercises

findings.finding: Grip strength in both dominant and non-dominant hands improved in both groups, but the added wrist and forearm exercises gave no significantly greater grip gain than the general periodised programme alone.
findings.population: 43 male high-school baseball players (mean 15.3 y), 12 wk

exercises.name: periodised resistance programme plus wrist and forearm exercises

findings.finding: With 3-5 sets of 10 at 10RM and 1-min inter-set rest for 12 weeks, continuous sets gave greater knee-extension 1RM (P<0.01) and maximal isometric strength (P<0.05) gains than identical sets split by a 30-s mid-set rest, which blunted acute lactate, GH and catecholamine responses.
findings.population: 26 men (9 NR, 9 WR, 8 control; training status not stated in abstract), 12 wk

exercises.name: knee extension, continuous 10RM sets (no intra-set rest)
knee extension, same sets with a 30-s rest at mid-set

findings.finding: Knee-extension muscular endurance improved more after 12 weeks of continuous 10RM sets than after the same sets interrupted by a 30-s mid-set rest (P<0.05); the abstract gives no magnitude or test details.
findings.population: 26 men (9 NR, 9 WR, 8 control; training status not stated in abstract), 12 wk

exercises.name: knee extension, continuous 10RM sets (no intra-set rest)
knee extension, same sets with a 30-s rest at mid-set

findings.finding: Muscle cross-sectional area rose markedly (P<0.01) with continuous sets but not with the 30-s intra-set rest regimen or in controls. The abstract does not state which muscle was imaged or the size of the change, so the muscle is left unknown.
findings.population: 26 men (9 NR, 9 WR, 8 control; training status not stated in abstract), 12 wk

exercises.name: lat pulldown, shoulder press, knee extension in continuous 10RM sets
same exercises with a 30-s rest at mid-set

findings.finding: 40 untrained men, 2 sessions/wk for 10 wk: full-ROM curls raised 1RM 25.7% vs 16.0% for partial ROM, a significantly larger gain (p<0.05); effect sizes 1.89 vs 0.87. Control +1.7%. 1RM was tested only at full ROM, which favours the full group.
findings.locator: Results, Table 1; Discussion (limitation). Full text read from an author-site PDF copy (paulogentil.com), not the publisher page
findings.population: 40 untrained young men, 10 weeks

exercises.name: full range-of-motion barbell preacher curl (0-130 deg elbow flexion)
partial range-of-motion barbell preacher curl (50-100 deg)

findings.finding: Ultrasound elbow-flexor thickness grew in both groups but not controls: 9.52% full vs 7.37% partial in Results (abstract gives 9.65% vs 7.83%). The difference was not significant (p=0.07); effect sizes 1.09 vs 0.57. The partial group lifted about 36% heavier loads.
findings.locator: Results paragraph 2, Figure 4; Discussion (p=0.07). Numbers in the abstract and Results text differ slightly
findings.population: 40 untrained young men, 10 weeks

exercises.name: full range-of-motion barbell preacher curl (0-130 deg elbow flexion)
partial range-of-motion barbell preacher curl (50-100 deg)

findings.finding: Resistance-trained college athletes squatted for 7 wk, and the authors tried to equate total work between groups. Adding elastic tension to the barbell raised back-squat 1RM by 16.47 kg vs 6.84 kg with free weight alone, a significant between-group difference (P<0.05). Longer-term effects were not studied.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 18550975). Full text paywalled (LWW HTTP 402, re-checked)
findings.population: 44 resistance-trained college athletes (men and women; basketball, wrestling, hockey), 7 weeks; elastic n=23, free-weight n=21

exercises.name: barbell back squat with added elastic bungee resistance (combined resistance)
barbell back squat with free weight only

findings.finding: Bench pressing with elastic band tension added to the barbell for 7 wk raised 1RM by 6.68 kg, vs 3.34 kg with free weight alone. The between-group difference was significant (P<0.05) in trained college athletes.
findings.population: 44 resistance-trained college athletes (men and women), 7 weeks

exercises.name: barbell bench press with added elastic bungee resistance (combined resistance)
barbell bench press with free weight only

findings.finding: Average power rose 68.55 W with combined elastic and free-weight training vs 23.66 W with free weight alone (P<0.05). SDs were large (84.35 and 40.56 W). The authors call this a lower-body power benefit; the abstract does not describe the power test or report a peak-power difference.
findings.population: 44 resistance-trained college athletes (men and women), 7 weeks

exercises.name: combined elastic + free-weight squat and bench training

findings.finding: Military men did 12 wk of neck-specific resistance training, 3 days/wk. Isometric and dynamic neck strength improved significantly, often by week 4, and kept rising to week 12. Results were compared with untrained controls, but the abstract gives no sample size, magnitudes or between-group statistics.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 17086765). Full text unavailable (no PMC; journal copy not open; DTIC report ADA497309 returned HTTP 403)
findings.population: military men, 12 weeks

findings.finding: Knee extensions to failure, 10 wk, untrained men. MRI quadriceps volume rose similarly with 30% 1RM x3 sets (+6.8±1.8%), 80% x1 (+3.2±0.8%) and 80% x3 (+7.2±1.9%), P=0.18; type I and II fibre area grew in all without group differences.
findings.locator: Results: Muscle hypertrophy; Fig. 1; Table 1 (fibre area). PMC3404827 full text
findings.population: 18 untrained young men (12 legs per condition), 10 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Knee-extension 1RM rose more after 80% 1RM training (1 or 3 sets) than after 30% 1RM x3 sets (P=0.04). Isometric MVC rose in all legs with no condition difference (80%x1 192→248, 80%x3 188→255, 30%x3 219→278 N·m).
findings.population: 18 untrained young men (12 legs per condition), 10 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Knee-extension peak power (80%x1 589→808 W; 80%x3 626→805 W; 30%x3 607→805 W) and isometric rate of torque development rose in every condition, with no between-condition differences.
findings.locator: Table 1 (peak power, RFD); Results: Muscle function
findings.population: 18 untrained young men (12 legs per condition), 10 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Reps to failure at 30% 1RM rose only in legs trained at 30% 1RM x3, which then completed more reps than legs trained at 80% (1 or 3 sets). Total work at 30% 1RM rose in all conditions without between-condition differences.
findings.population: 18 untrained young men (12 legs per condition), 10 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: High-load endurance test: reps to failure at 80% 1RM rose in all conditions (10-11 to 12-13) without group differences, but total work at 80% 1RM increased significantly less after 30% 1RM training than after either 80% condition.
findings.population: 18 untrained young men (12 legs per condition), 10 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Seven untrained men did only bench press (75% 1RM, 3x10, 3/wk) for 24 wk, no control group. Pectoralis major thickness rose 21.1→30.2 mm (significant from week 1, rising throughout); triceps 34.2→40.1 mm (significant from week 5, gains mostly before ~week 15).
findings.locator: Results; Table I; Fig. 1. PMC3831787 full text
findings.population: 7 untrained young men, 24 wk bench press only, 3 sessions/wk

exercises.name: free-weight bench press (75% 1RM, 3x10, grip 200% biacromial width)

findings.finding: Seven untrained men, 24 wk of bench press only, no control. Biceps thickness went 25.1→26.0 mm; the overall time effect was significant (p=0.035), but no comparison with baseline or within any phase passed the Bonferroni-corrected threshold.
findings.population: 7 untrained young men, 24 wk bench press only, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Bench press 1RM rose from 51.0 to 77.4 kg over 24 weeks of bench press training. The rise was significant from week 3 and in each analysed phase (weeks 0-6, 6-15, 15-24). There was no control group.
findings.population: 7 untrained young men, 24 wk bench press only, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Untrained women, 6 wk leg press, squat, knee extension. Normal-speed 6-10RM (~80-85% 1RM) enlarged type I, IIA and IIX fibres; slow-speed 6-10RM (~40-60% 1RM) enlarged only IIA and IIX. The abstract gives no fibre-size result for 20-30RM and no between-group statistics.
findings.locator: Abstract only (PubMed 22328004). Springer and ProQuest full text are paywalled, and I found no open repository copy. The abstract does not name the biopsied muscle and gives no numeric CSA values.
findings.population: 34 untrained women, 6 wk (2 sessions/wk in week 1, then 3/wk)

exercises.name: leg press, squat and knee extension at 6-10RM, normal speed (~80-85% 1RM)
leg press, squat and knee extension at 6-10RM, slow speed (10 s up / 4 s down, ~40-60% 1RM)
leg press, squat and knee extension at 20-30RM, normal speed (~40-60% 1RM)

findings.finding: Deep squat (0-120°) enlarged front-thigh MRI CSA at all six analysed sites (4-7%); shallow (0-60°) only at the two most proximal, with deep gains larger at every site. Leg lean mass: deep +2.0±0.8% (significant), shallow +1.5±0.9% (not); body composition did not differ between groups.
findings.locator: Results: Thigh muscle CSA and Lean body mass; Figs 4-5. Author accepted manuscript, Brage NIH repository (hdl.handle.net/11250/218859, now on NVA). Front thigh = quadriceps + sartorius, with adductors in proximal slices.
findings.population: 17 male sports-science students who had squatted no more than once a week in the prior 6 months (deep 8, shallow 9), 12 wk, 3 sessions/wk, periodized (Mon 3x10RM→3x6RM, Fri 4x5RM→5x3RM, Wed submaximal)

findings.finding: Back-thigh (hamstring) MRI CSA increased at only one site (the second most proximal) after deep squat training, and at no site after shallow squat training. The paper reports no between-group test for back-thigh CSA, so neither depth can be called superior.
findings.locator: Results: Thigh muscle CSA; Fig. 4 lower panel; Discussion
findings.population: 17 male sports-science students (deep 8, shallow 9), 12 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Deep squat raised 1RM ~20±3% in both depths; shallow squat raised shallow 1RM 36±4%, deep 1RM 9±2%; each group gained more in its trained range (P<0.05). Only deep squat raised isometric knee-extension torque (75°: 6±2%; 105°: 8±1%, exceeding shallow's 0±5%).
findings.population: 17 male sports-science students (deep 8, shallow 9), 12 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Squat-jump height rose 15±3% after deep squat training, significantly more than after shallow squat training. Countermovement jump improved in both groups (shallow 7±4%, deep 13±2%) with no between-group difference.
findings.locator: Results: Jump height; Fig. 6 (jump height figure)
findings.population: 17 male sports-science students (deep 8, shallow 9), 12 wk, 3 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Trained men, 8 wk, volume load matched, sets to failure. Biceps thickness grew equally with bodybuilding-type 3x10RM, 90 s rest, split routine (+12.6%, 34.5→38.7 mm) and powerlifting-type 7x3RM, 3 min rest, total-body (+12.7%, 35.3→39.6 mm). Sessions took ~17 vs ~70 min.
findings.locator: Results: Muscle Thickness; Table 4; Fig. 1. Full published PDF hosted on co-author B. Contreras's website. The biceps were trained only through pulldowns and rows, and no other muscle was measured.
findings.population: 17 resistance-trained young men (4.2±2.4 yr experience; bodybuilding-type 9, powerlifting-type 8), 8 wk, 3 sessions/wk

exercises.name: bodybuilding-type split routine, 3x10RM, 90 s rest (presses, pulldowns, row, squat, leg press, leg extension)
powerlifting-type total-body routine, 7x3RM, 3 min rest (same 9 exercises)

findings.finding: Bench press 1RM rose 10.9% (104.8→116.2 kg) with 7x3RM versus 8.1% (97.1→105.1 kg) with 3x10RM. Unadjusted gains did not differ; with baseline as covariate the heavy protocol was significantly better (p≤0.05). Two of 10 heavy-protocol starters left with joint injuries.

quadriceps resistance training in shortened range (0-50° knee flexion)

exercises.name: quadriceps resistance training in lengthened range (40-90° knee flexion)
quadriceps resistance training in shortened range (0-50° knee flexion)

partial range of motion isokinetic knee extension

partial range of motion isokinetic knee extension

findings.finding: Elbow-extension 1RM rose 40.1±21.3% after cable push-downs and 44.5±20.1% after overhead cable extensions. ANCOVA found no difference between conditions (p=0.640, eta2=0.015).

findings.finding: Trained men trained elbow extension three times weekly for 8 weeks over a partial (45-90 degrees) or full (0-120 degrees) range; the acute protocol was 3x8 at 8RM. Triceps CSA rose 48.7±14.5% with partial and 28.2±10.9% with full ROM, significantly more with partial.

full range of motion elbow extension (0-120 degrees)

full range of motion elbow extension (0-120 degrees)

full range of motion elbow extension (0-120 degrees)

findings.finding: Adding 30 s passive stretching between sets raised vastus lateralis thickness 17.0% versus 7.3% (significant group-by-time interaction, p≤0.02). Rectus femoris rose 12.4% versus 9.1%, with no interaction reported. The authors say the data cannot establish stretching is superior.

traditional strength training plus 30 s passive static stretching between sets

findings.finding: Biceps thickness rose 7.2% with inter-set stretching and 4.7% without it; triceps thickness rose 12.3% and 7.1%. Both groups improved. A group interaction is reported only for vastus lateralis and the four-site sum (10.5% vs 6.7%).

exercises.name: traditional strength training (including biceps curl and elbow extension)
traditional strength training plus 30 s passive static stretching between sets

traditional strength training plus 30 s passive static stretching between sets

findings.finding: Calf raises taken to failure with light (20-30RM) or heavy (6-10RM) loads grew the calves by a similar amount. Light minus heavy was 0.2 mm for soleus (90% CI -0.3 to 0.7), medial gastrocnemius (-0.2 to 0.8) and lateral gastrocnemius (-0.5 to 0.8).

seated and standing calf raises with heavy load (6-10RM)

findings.finding: Medial gastrocnemius thickness: unilateral seated leg-press calf raises (3-4 sets x 20-25 reps, 9 wk) grew most with toes out (+8.4%) vs forward (+5.8%) and in (+3.8%). The abstract reports the out-vs-in gap as significant (p<0.05); no other pairwise difference is reported.

findings.finding: Upper pectoralis (2nd intercostal site): incline-only (44 deg) pressing grew thickness more than flat-only (adjusted difference 0.62 cm, 95% CI 0.23-1.0, p=0.003) and the flat+incline combination (0.50 cm, 0.14-0.86, p=0.008). Ultrasound subsample n=30.

findings.population: 23 moderately active college students (10 men, 13 women), single session

findings.finding: In leg extensions (8 reps at 70% of 8RM), medial leg rotation (toes in) gave the highest normalized RMS EMG for vastus lateralis and vastus medialis of the three positions tested. The abstract reports no values or pairwise tests.
findings.population: 24 men and women, mean age 23.7 y

exercises.name: leg extension, legs medially rotated (toes in)
leg extension, legs laterally rotated (toes out)

findings.finding: Lateral leg rotation (toes out) during leg extension gave the highest normalized RMS EMG for rectus femoris of the three positions tested. The abstract gives no values, effect sizes or pairwise tests. This is activation only.
findings.population: 24 men and women, mean age 23.7 y

exercises.name: leg extension, legs laterally rotated (toes out)
leg extension, legs medially rotated (toes in)

findings.finding: In isometric flat-bench holds, a supinated (reverse) grip raised EMG in biceps brachii and the clavicular (upper) pectoralis major compared with pronated grips. The abstract gives no amplitudes; the author described grip-width effects as small.
findings.population: 12 healthy men; 5 isometric bench-press grip variants

exercises.name: flat bench press isometric hold, supinated (reverse) grip
flat bench press isometric hold, pronated grip

findings.finding: Moving from a wide grip toward a narrow grip increased lateral-head triceps EMG during isometric bench holds, with or without forearm supination. The abstract reports no amplitudes.
findings.population: 12 healthy men; 5 isometric bench-press grip variants

exercises.name: flat bench press isometric hold, narrow grip
flat bench press isometric hold, mid grip
flat bench press isometric hold, wide grip

findings.finding: With a pronated grip, narrowing from wide lowered EMG of the sternal pectoralis major (termed sternoclavicular in the abstract). With a supinated grip, narrowing did not lower it. The author called grip-width effects small and advised choosing grip for sport specificity.
findings.population: 12 healthy men; 5 isometric bench-press grip variants

exercises.name: flat bench press isometric hold, wide pronated grip
flat bench press isometric hold, narrow pronated grip

findings.finding: Biceps EMG (lifting-phase values) was highest in upright row (0.925), then behind-neck pulldown (0.680), front pulldown (0.650), bent-over row (0.444) and seated row (0.420). With phases pooled, upright row beat bent-over and seated row (p<0.001) and behind-neck pulldown (p<0.05); front pulldown beat bent-over row (p<0.05).
findings.population: 8 weight-trained men, mean age 20.4 y; 3 reps at 70% 1RM, overhand grip

findings.finding: Latissimus EMG was higher for seated row (0.826), front pulldown (0.781) and behind-neck pulldown than for bent-over row (0.641) (p<0.001 to p<0.05). All four beat upright row (0.136; p<0.001). The paper's table and figure disagree on the behind-neck value.
findings.population: 8 weight-trained men, mean age 20.4 y; 3 reps at 70% 1RM, overhand grip

findings.finding: Upper trapezius EMG was highest for upright row (0.829) and bent-over row (0.775). Both were significantly above seated row (0.435), front pulldown (0.285) and behind-neck pulldown (0.279), at p<0.01 to p<0.001.
findings.population: 8 weight-trained men, mean age 20.4 y; 3 reps at 70% 1RM, overhand grip

findings.finding: Middle trapezius EMG peaked in bent-over row (0.892). That was above front pulldown (0.485) and behind-neck pulldown (0.500) at p<0.001, and above upright row (0.665) at p<0.05. Seated row (0.664) beat front pulldown (p<0.05).
findings.population: 8 weight-trained men, mean age 20.4 y; 3 reps at 70% 1RM, overhand grip

findings.finding: Lower trapezius EMG was highest in bent-over row (0.869). It was above front pulldown (0.554) at p<0.001, and above upright row (0.669), seated row (0.566) and behind-neck pulldown (0.527) at p<0.01.
findings.population: 8 weight-trained men, mean age 20.4 y; 3 reps at 70% 1RM, overhand grip

findings.finding: Upper and lower rectus abdominis and internal oblique EMG (normalized to MVC) were highest for Power Wheel pike, knee-up and roll-out, hanging knee-up with straps, and 30-degree inclined reverse crunch. The tested set also included crunch and bent-knee sit-up. No values in abstract.
findings.population: 21 healthy men and women aged 23-43 y

findings.finding: External oblique EMG was highest for Power Wheel pike, knee-up and roll-out and for hanging knee-up with straps among the exercises tested. The abstract gives no numbers.
findings.population: 21 healthy men and women aged 23-43 y

findings.finding: Among the abdominal exercises tested, latissimus dorsi EMG was highest for Power Wheel pike, knee-up and roll-out, hanging knee-up with straps, and 30-degree inclined reverse crunch. The abstract gives no values.
findings.population: 21 healthy men and women aged 23-43 y

findings.finding: Rectus femoris (hip flexor) EMG was highest for Power Wheel pike and knee-up, 30-degree inclined reverse crunch and bent-knee sit-up. The authors warn this hip-flexor demand may be a problem for some people with low back problems.
findings.population: 21 healthy men and women aged 23-43 y

findings.finding: Lumbar paraspinal EMG was low and similar across all the traditional and device-based abdominal exercises tested. No exercise stood out for lower-back activation.
findings.population: 21 healthy men and women aged 23-43 y

findings.finding: With hands on a Swiss ball, triceps EMG rose in push-ups (43.1 vs 22.2 %MVC, p=.002) and in push-up plus (29.6 vs 18.7, p=.024). Feet on the ball made no difference (29.9 vs 32.7, p=.355).
findings.population: 13 healthy college men with >6 months weight-training experience; single session

exercises.name: push-up plus, hands on Swiss ball

findings.finding: Pectoralis major EMG did not change with a Swiss ball under the hands (26.65 vs 21.4 %MVC, p=.341) or under the feet (29.9 vs 30.4, p=.717), or in push-up plus (21.4 vs 14.0, p=.079). Only stable-vs-unstable pairs were tested.
findings.population: 13 healthy college men with >6 months weight-training experience; single session

exercises.name: push-up plus, hands on Swiss ball

findings.finding: Rectus abdominis EMG rose with hands on the Swiss ball in push-ups (22.6 vs 13.4 %MVC, p=.001) and in push-up plus (25.4 vs 14.9, p=.011). Feet on the ball made no difference (19.6 vs 19.2, p=.742).
findings.population: 13 healthy college men with >6 months weight-training experience; single session

exercises.name: push-up plus, hands on Swiss ball

findings.finding: The Swiss ball raised external oblique EMG only in the push-up plus (23.9 vs 19.2 %MVC, reported significant). Standard push-ups with hands on the ball (24.07 vs 20.9, p=.119) or feet on the ball (26.7 vs 27.79, p=.575) showed no change.
findings.population: 13 healthy college men with >6 months weight-training experience; single session

exercises.name: push-up plus, hands on Swiss ball

findings.finding: At 75% MVC isometric abduction, only the deltoid was active (pectoralis, latissimus <10% MVC); it was the only task recruiting all seven deltoid segments. Middle segments D2-D5 reached 73-88 %MVC versus 38-58 for D1, D6, D7 (p<0.05).
findings.population: 20 healthy men aged 18-30 y; isometric force impulses at 75% MVC, arm at 20 degrees abduction

findings.finding: In isometric flexion, anterior deltoid D1-D2 (55 %MVC each) and clavicular pectoral P1-P2 (42, 33) were prime movers; lower pectoral segments reached 24-31. In extension, D1-D2 and all pectoral segments except P3 (11 %MVC) were silent.
findings.population: 20 healthy men aged 18-30 y; isometric force impulses at 75% MVC, arm at 20 degrees abduction

findings.finding: In isometric extension, latissimus L2-L3 and posterior deltoid D5-D7 were most active (about 73 %MVC; D6 81, D7 84) versus about 42 for other active segments. In flexion, D5-D7 and L2-L6 were silent; L1 reached 11 %MVC.
findings.population: 20 healthy men aged 18-30 y; isometric force impulses at 75% MVC, arm at 20 degrees abduction

findings.finding: In isometric adduction, all six latissimus segments (55-79 %MVC) and lower pectoral P4-P6 (56-66) exceeded upper pectoral P1-P3 (33-41); deltoid activity was limited to D6-D7 (28, 47). In abduction, pectoral and latissimus segments were silent (<10% MVC).
findings.population: 20 healthy men aged 18-30 y; isometric force impulses at 75% MVC, arm at 20 degrees abduction

findings.finding: In 22 healthy young adults, the Ab-Slide produced the greatest peak normalized EMG for the abdominal muscles measured (rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques) of four exercises. Six Bonferroni-significant pairwise differences occurred; the abstract does not identify them or give values.
findings.population: 10 healthy young men and 12 healthy young women

findings.finding: Fine-wire brachioradialis EMG during elbow flexion at 0, 22, 45 and 67 N loads showed no difference between neutral, pronated and supinated forearm positions, so grip orientation did not change brachioradialis activation. The abstract reports brachioradialis EMG only.
findings.population: 10 healthy adults (9 men, 1 woman; mean age 34 ± 10 y)

exercises.name: elbow flexion with neutral forearm (hammer grip)

findings.finding: During elbow flexion, brachioradialis activation was significantly higher in the concentric (lifting) phase, at 23±5% MVIC, than in the eccentric (lowering) phase, at 11±5% MVIC.
findings.population: 10 healthy adults (9 men, 1 woman; mean age 34 ± 10 y)

findings.finding: With the elbow at 90 degrees and the two heaviest rotation loads (18 and 27 N), brachioradialis EMG was significantly greater in concentric pronation and eccentric supination than in concentric supination and eccentric pronation. The authors read this as a secondary pronator role.
findings.population: 10 healthy adults (9 men, 1 woman; mean age 34 ± 10 y)

findings.finding: On Tergumed trunk-extension devices, EMG of the back muscles generally rose significantly from 30% to 50% to 70% of maximum mean torque. At 30% and 50% the back muscles already exceeded the authors' 60% MVIC threshold, an EMG benchmark rather than measured strength gain.
findings.population: 30 healthy participants

exercises.name: trunk extension machine at 30% maximum mean torque
trunk extension machine at 50% maximum mean torque
trunk extension machine at 70% maximum mean torque

findings.finding: On the Tergumed trunk-flexion device, abdominal muscle EMG generally rose significantly with resistance from 30% to 50% to 70% of maximum mean torque. Only the 70% load was judged to take the abdominals past the authors' 60% MVIC threshold (EMG only).
findings.population: 30 healthy participants

exercises.name: trunk flexion machine at 30% maximum mean torque
trunk flexion machine at 50% maximum mean torque
trunk flexion machine at 70% maximum mean torque

findings.finding: Unlike the other back muscles, lumbar multifidus was highly active during both trunk-extension and trunk-flexion device exercises. The abstract gives no values and does not statistically compare the two conditions, so neither is favoured.
findings.population: 30 healthy participants

findings.finding: In women with trapezius myalgia, trapezius EMG was highest for shrugs (102±11% MVC), lateral raises (97±6%) and upright rows (85±5%) of five exercises. Lateral raises and upright rows needed 3–10 kg; shrugs needed 20–30 kg. Most exercises exceeded 60% MVC.
findings.population: 12 female workers aged 30-60 y with clinically diagnosed trapezius myalgia (chronic neck muscle pain)

findings.finding: Biceps femoris EMG, rectus femoris EMG and the hamstring-to-quadriceps EMG ratio all differed significantly across the six exercises (P<0.001). 'Favours' is empty only because the abstract names no top exercise and gives no values; it does not mean no difference.
findings.population: 34 college athletes (women and men)

findings.finding: Biceps femoris RMS EMG and its ratios to rectus femoris and vastus lateralis differed significantly across the five exercises, with no sex-by-exercise interaction for biceps femoris (p=0.67). 'Favours' is empty because the abstract names no top exercise, not for lack of difference.
findings.population: 20 athletes and recreationally active college students (men and women)

findings.finding: Rectus femoris and vastus lateralis RMS EMG differed significantly across the five exercises, with no sex-by-exercise interaction (RF p=0.53, VL p=0.06). 'Favours' is empty because the abstract gives no ranking or per-exercise values, not for lack of difference.
findings.population: 20 athletes and recreationally active college students (men and women)

findings.finding: Wider back-squat stances raised gluteus maximus EMG: at 70% 1RM, 200% vs 100% of inter-trochanter width was higher (0.0288 vs 0.0205 mV; ES 1.34), 150% also exceeded 100% (ES 0.5); similar at 0% 1RM (ES 1.07, 0.65); no difference at 30% 1RM.
findings.population: 6 experienced male lifters (3 y lifting), single session, 0/30/70% 1RM

exercises.name: back squat, stance 100% of inter-trochanter distance
back squat, stance 150% of inter-trochanter distance
back squat, stance 200% of inter-trochanter distance

findings.finding: Stance width produced no significant EMG differences (p>0.05) in vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, rectus femoris, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, gluteus medius or adductor magnus at 0, 30 or 70% 1RM; only gluteus maximus responded to stance.
findings.population: 6 experienced male lifters (3 y lifting), single session, 0/30/70% 1RM

exercises.name: back squat, stance 100% of inter-trochanter distance
back squat, stance 150% of inter-trochanter distance
back squat, stance 200% of inter-trochanter distance

findings.finding: Mean EMG of all eight thigh muscles rose with squat load from unloaded to 30% to 70% 1RM at every stance (e.g., vastus lateralis 0.0441 to 0.0605 mV at narrow stance); no load-effect p-values were reported and EMG was unnormalized.
findings.population: 6 experienced male lifters (3 y lifting), single session

findings.finding: Left latissimus pull-phase EMG was higher in the inverted row (64.8% MVC) than bent-over row (53.4%) and right-hand-only cable row (15.4%, non-pulling side); right latissimus, the cable row's pulling side, showed no reported exercise effect, only pull above lowering (82.2 vs 53.8%).
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Peak Muscle Activation; Figure 4
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: Left thoracic erector spinae (T9) pull-phase EMG was 90.9% MVC in the inverted row versus 72.8% bent-over row and 14.8% right-hand-only cable row (non-pulling side); right thoracic erector spinae showed no significant exercise differences.
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Peak Muscle Activation; Figure 4
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: Lumbar erector spinae (L3) EMG was highest in the barbell bent-over row (right 42.5%, left 43.3% MVC), intermediate in the inverted row (29.9%, 28.7%) and lowest in the one-arm cable row (17.3%, 14.7%).
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Peak Muscle Activation; Figure 4
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: Right gluteus maximus EMG was similar in the inverted row (19.2% MVC) and bent-over row (19.0%), both above the one-arm cable row (8.5%); right gluteus medius was higher in the inverted row (19.9%) than the cable row (10.7%), bent-over row (13.7%) not differing from inverted.
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Peak Muscle Activation; Figure 4
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: Biceps femoris EMG was 25.7% MVC in the inverted row, significantly above the bent-over row (12.5%), which in turn exceeded the one-arm cable row (1.9%).
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Peak Muscle Activation
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: The one-arm (right-hand) cable row raised left external oblique (9.3% MVC vs 4.2% bent-over, 3.8% inverted) and right internal oblique (20.8% vs 13.3%, 12.0%); rectus abdominis, right external and left internal oblique showed no exercise effect.
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Peak Muscle Activation; Figure 4
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: Rectus femoris EMG was low in all rows: one-arm cable row 11.5% MVC and bent-over row 8.2% (not different), with the cable row significantly above the inverted row (2.7%).
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Peak Muscle Activation; Figure 4
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: Modelled L4/L5 compression was highest in the bent-over row (3576 N; n=6 after one exclusion) versus one-arm cable row (2457 N) and inverted row (2339 N); the bent-over row also had most lumbar flexion (22.9°) and greatest flexion-extension muscular stiffness (3244 N·m/rad).
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Raw and Normalized Spine Position and Comparison of Spinal Loading and Stiffness; Figures 5-7
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men (compression data n=6), load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: Despite neutral-spine instructions, the one-arm cable row produced the most lumbar twist: a mean 67.7% of participants' maximum twist range versus 19.3% (inverted row) and 25.2% (bent-over row); axial twist muscular stiffness was higher in the cable row but not significantly.
findings.locator: Results, Comparison of Raw and Normalized Spine Position; Figure 5B; Figure 7 caption; Discussion
findings.population: 7 healthy recreationally active men, load-matched rows, single session

findings.finding: At 80% 1RM, latissimus dorsi EMG did not differ between behind-the-neck, front-of-the-neck and V-bar pulldowns (technique p=0.777); concentric exceeded eccentric. EMG was normalized to each subject's highest technique/phase value, not to MVC.

findings.population: 24 weight-trained men (>=1 y), 3 central reps of 5 at 80% 1RM

exercises.name: V-bar lat pulldown (wide grip, frontal-plane adduction as defined by authors)

findings.finding: Pectoralis major concentric EMG ranked front-of-the-neck > V-bar > behind-the-neck pulldown. The Results text reports no eccentric-phase differences, whereas the abstract claims front and V-bar exceeded behind-the-neck eccentrically; treat eccentric claim as inconsistent.
findings.population: 24 weight-trained men (>=1 y), 80% 1RM

exercises.name: V-bar lat pulldown (wide grip, frontal-plane adduction as defined by authors)

findings.finding: Posterior deltoid concentric EMG was higher in the behind-the-neck pulldown than front-of-the-neck and V-bar, with front-of-the-neck above V-bar; eccentrically only behind-the-neck exceeded V-bar (technique p<0.01, interaction p<0.05).
findings.population: 24 weight-trained men (>=1 y), 80% 1RM

exercises.name: V-bar lat pulldown (wide grip, frontal-plane adduction as defined by authors)

findings.finding: Biceps brachii EMG was highest in the behind-the-neck pulldown, intermediate with the V-bar and lowest in the front-of-the-neck pulldown, in both concentric and eccentric phases (technique p<0.001).
findings.population: 24 weight-trained men (>=1 y), 80% 1RM

exercises.name: V-bar lat pulldown (wide grip, frontal-plane adduction as defined by authors)

findings.finding: After expert cueing (lat palpation, pull with the back, retract scapulae), pulldown latissimus dorsi EMG rose from 71.1% to 83.59% of peak isometric (p=0.005, 17.6% change); teres major rose 42.69% to 50.79%, not significant (p=0.09).
findings.locator: Results section; Figure 3 (full text via Internet Archive copy of publisher page)

exercises.name: front wide-grip lat pulldown, basic instruction
front wide-grip lat pulldown, lat-focused expert instruction

findings.finding: Cueing to use the back rather than the arms did not lower biceps brachii EMG during the pulldown (30.45% vs 31.36% of peak isometric), so the added lat activity was not isolation of the back muscles.
findings.population: 8 untrained women (18-35 y), load 30% of MVIC

exercises.name: front wide-grip lat pulldown, basic instruction
front wide-grip lat pulldown, lat-focused expert instruction

findings.finding: At 50% 1RM, standing on a BOSU versus stable ground produced no significant difference in rectus abdominis, external oblique, transversus/internal oblique or erector spinae EMG in the back squat, deadlift, overhead press or curl.
findings.locator: Results section; Figures 2-5; Discussion (full text via Internet Archive copy of EIU repository PDF)

exercises.name: back squat, deadlift, overhead press and curl on BOSU at 50% 1RM
same lifts on stable ground at 50% 1RM

findings.finding: Stable-ground lifting at 75% 1RM exceeded BOSU at 50% 1RM for rectus abdominis in the overhead press (about 10% MVC) and transversus/internal oblique in the overhead press and curl; external oblique and erector spinae did not differ between these conditions.
findings.locator: Results, Rectus Abdominis and Transversus/Internal Oblique subsections; Figures 2 and 4
findings.population: 12 resistance-trained men (>=4 y)

findings.finding: Erector spinae EMG, pooled across surfaces and loads, was greatest in the deadlift, then the back squat (roughly 45-65% MVC for both), each above the overhead press and curl, which did not differ (p=.07); surface and load had no effect.
findings.locator: Results, Erector Spinae subsection; Figure 5; Discussion
findings.population: 12 resistance-trained men (>=4 y)

findings.finding: External oblique EMG (pooled across conditions) was higher in overhead press than squat, deadlift or curl; transversus/internal oblique activity in overhead press and curl exceeded squat and deadlift at stable 75% 1RM, and overhead press did so at stable 50%; BOSU showed no lift differences.
findings.locator: Results, External Oblique and Transversus/Internal Oblique subsections; Figures 3-4
findings.population: 12 resistance-trained men (>=4 y)

findings.finding: Across three standard hamstring exercises, internally rotating the foot raised the medial-to-lateral hamstring EMG ratio (medial bias) and externally rotating it lowered the ratio (lateral/biceps femoris bias); joint range of motion was unaffected. No numeric values or statistics accessible.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed); Results and Discussion snippets on archived ScienceDirect page; full text paywalled
findings.population: 13 healthy active adults (6 men), mean age 27.7 y

exercises.name: hamstring exercises with foot internally rotated
hamstring exercises with foot externally rotated

findings.finding: The one-legged deadlift showed a higher medial-to-lateral hamstring activation ratio than the other two exercises and was the only one favouring medial hamstrings with the foot straight; exact values and the third exercise could not be read.
findings.locator: Discussion snippet on archived ScienceDirect abstract page (main findings); full text paywalled
findings.population: 13 healthy active adults (6 men), mean age 27.7 y

exercises.name: third hamstring exercise (not named in accessible text)

findings.finding: Across crunches loaded at 20-100% of 1RM, averaged abdominal EMG (rectus abdominis and external oblique, RMS of the first repetition) was, in general, significantly greater at 100% 1RM; loads 20% 1RM apart, e.g. 20 vs 40%, mostly did not differ.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results and Conclusion); full text paywalled, not read

findings.finding: Biceps long-head surface EMG did not differ significantly between incline and standing dumbbell curls in any third of elbow range, concentric or eccentric; both rose to about 95% of MVC RMS in the final concentric third.
findings.population: 22 right-handed men engaged in strength training for at least 1 year (23.0 +/- 3.5 y), one concentric-eccentric cycle at 40% of isometric MVC

findings.finding: Preacher curl biceps long-head EMG exceeded incline and standing curls in the first concentric third but was lower in the final third (peak about 80% MVC RMS, early); its first eccentric third was also lower, confining high activation to a narrow elbow range.
findings.population: 22 right-handed men engaged in strength training for at least 1 year (23.0 +/- 3.5 y), one concentric-eccentric cycle at 40% of isometric MVC

findings.finding: During anterior lat pulldowns at 70% 1RM, a pronated grip produced significantly greater MVIC-normalized latissimus dorsi EMG than a supinated grip (p<0.05); the authors recommend a pronated grip regardless of grip width.

findings.locator: Abstract (Results); full text paywalled, not read

findings.finding: Concentric-phase medial deltoid EMG was greater on the free-weight bench press than the Smith machine bench press (tested at 70% and 90% 1RM, experienced and inexperienced pressers); sample size and effect sizes not given in abstract.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results); full text paywalled, not read

findings.finding: Muscle activation (measured: pectoralis major, anterior and medial deltoid) was greater at 90% 1RM than at 70% 1RM, 2 repetitions each; per-muscle breakdown not given in the abstract.

findings.locator: Abstract (Results and Conclusion); full text paywalled, not read

findings.population: 25 young adults (21 men, 4 women)

findings.finding: Rotating Perfect Pullup handles produced no EMG differences versus conventional pull-up or chin-up for any muscle measured (latissimus, biceps, infraspinatus 71-79%, lower trapezius, pectoralis major, erector spinae 39-41%, external oblique 31-35% MVIC).

findings.finding: Pointing the feet neutral, 45° in or 45° out during 45° leg-press calf raises did not change soleus, medial or lateral gastrocnemius RMS EMG. Foot-position effect F=0.27, P=0.75, partial eta squared 0.003; interaction F=0.09, P=1.00.
findings.population: 10 strength-trained men aged 20-30 y, 1 set of 5 reps at 10RM load per foot position

exercises.name: 45° leg-press calf raise, feet 45° internally rotated
45° leg-press calf raise, feet 45° externally rotated

findings.finding: In the knee-straight 45° leg-press calf raise, soleus RMS was lower than both gastrocnemius heads regardless of foot position (muscle effect F=17.86, P=0.003, partial eta squared 0.31; no interaction). RMS was not MVC-normalised, so between-muscle amplitude comparisons are weak.
findings.population: 10 strength-trained men aged 20-30 y, 1 set of 5 reps at 10RM load per foot position

exercises.name: 45° leg-press calf raise (knee extended), all foot positions

findings.finding: With 8RM loads, gluteus maximus EMG was higher in the modified single-leg squat (65.6% MVIC) than the stiff-leg deadlift (40.5%) or bilateral squat (40.3%) (p<0.001). Stiff-leg deadlift and bilateral squat did not differ.

findings.finding: Hamstring EMG was highest in the modified single-leg squat (40.1% MVIC). It beat the stiff-leg deadlift (29.9%; p=0.001), and the stiff-leg deadlift beat the bilateral squat (24.4%; p=0.004). In every exercise, gluteus maximus EMG was higher than hamstring EMG.
findings.population: 18 resistance-trained young adult women, one session, 3 reps at 8RM

findings.finding: At 1RM, gluteus maximus EMG (normalised to MVIC) was higher in the barbell hip thrust than in the back squat (ES 1.39, p=0.038).
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed/publisher); full text paywalled and repository copy embargoed
findings.population: 8 men with at least 1 year of lower-body strength training; 60 kg and 1RM trials

findings.finding: At 1RM, gluteus maximus EMG did not differ significantly between the barbell hip thrust and the Romanian deadlift (ES 0.49, p=0.285). The authors concluded that both isolate the hip extensors about equally well.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed/publisher); full text paywalled and repository copy embargoed
findings.population: 8 men with at least 1 year of lower-body strength training; 60 kg and 1RM trials

findings.finding: At 1RM, vastus lateralis EMG was higher in the back squat than in the Romanian deadlift (ES 1.36, p=0.002) and the barbell hip thrust (ES 2.27, p=0.009).
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed/publisher); full text paywalled and repository copy embargoed
findings.population: 8 men with at least 1 year of lower-body strength training; 60 kg and 1RM trials

findings.finding: In the prone leg curl, internal foot rotation raised medial hamstring EMG over neutral (concentric +8.7%, eccentric +5.9% MVC; p<0.01; d=0.88-0.99). External rotation lowered it (concentric -5.8%, eccentric -5.2% MVC; p<0.05; d=0.67-0.92).

prone leg curl with neutral foot
prone leg curl with external foot rotation

Nordic hamstring exercise (neutral, internal or external foot rotation)

findings.finding: At 30% of body mass, the barbell pullover gave higher %MVIC than the straight-arm pulldown at either grip in the upper, middle and lower pectoralis major (p<=0.01). Example, lower pec concentric RMS: 191.97 µV versus 104.46 and 117.03 µV.
findings.population: 20 physically active adults with at least 1 year of resistance training (mean age 26); one set of 8 reps at 30% body mass

findings.finding: The straight-arm pulldown at either grip gave higher latissimus dorsi %MVIC than the barbell pullover (p<=0.001), about 18% MVIC. Concentric RMS was 151.26 and 159.40 µV in the pulldown versus 54.12 µV in the pullover.
findings.population: 20 physically active adults with at least 1 year of resistance training (mean age 26); one set of 8 reps at 30% body mass

findings.finding: Triceps brachii (medial head) %MVIC did not differ significantly between the barbell pullover and the straight-arm pulldown at either grip (p>0.05). Triceps was among the most active muscles in every exercise, at about 19% MVIC in the pulldown.
findings.population: 20 physically active adults with at least 1 year of resistance training (mean age 26); one set of 8 reps at 30% body mass

findings.finding: Rectus abdominis %MVIC was higher in the barbell pullover than in the straight-arm pulldown at either grip (p<=0.01). At about 18% MVIC it was the most active muscle in the pullover, though not significantly above triceps or pectoralis.
findings.population: 20 physically active adults with at least 1 year of resistance training (mean age 26); one set of 8 reps at 30% body mass

findings.finding: Anterior deltoid %MVIC was higher in the barbell pullover than in the straight-arm pulldown (p<=0.01). Even so, the anterior deltoid was the least active muscle measured in all three exercises.
findings.population: 20 physically active adults with at least 1 year of resistance training (mean age 26); one set of 8 reps at 30% body mass

findings.finding: In the straight-arm pulldown, widening the grip from 100% to 150% of biacromial width did not significantly change EMG in any measured muscle: the pectoralis major portions, latissimus dorsi, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii and rectus abdominis.
findings.population: 20 physically active adults with at least 1 year of resistance training (mean age 26); one set of 8 reps at 30% body mass

findings.finding: MRI of 4 healthy adults showed the anterior entrance of the subacromial space was smaller with the shoulder girdle held protracted than held retracted. Static positions only; no exercise, load, muscle or symptom outcome.
findings.locator: Abstract (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 4 healthy adults (PubMed MeSH lists both sexes; ages not given in abstract)

findings.finding: Dissection found upper and middle trapezius fibres run largely horizontally, which the authors say rules out direct scapular elevation. They instead pull scapula and clavicle backward, or lift the scapula by rotating the clavicle. Fibres from C7, T1 and the lower half of ligamentum nuchae had the most volume. Anatomical inference only; no EMG.

findings.population: cadaveric specimens (number not given in abstract)

exercises.name: scapular raising via clavicular rotation at the sternoclavicular joint

findings.finding: Cadaveric simulation of scapular-plane abduction: supraspinatus supplied relatively more force early in the arc, middle deltoid more near the top. With simulated supraspinatus paralysis, middle deltoid force rose most from 15 to 45 degrees. Tendon excursion: middle deltoid 6.4 cm, supraspinatus 3.8 cm.
findings.locator: Abstract (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)

scapular-plane glenohumeral abduction, late part of the range

findings.finding: In 2 cadaver arms plus a computer model, the biceps' elbow-flexion leverage was greatest at a fairly extended elbow angle, and that maximum was bigger in supination. Its supination leverage shrank as the elbow straightened. Leverage data only, not EMG or training.
findings.locator: Abstract (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 2 anatomic specimens plus a computer model of the elbow

exercises.name: elbow flexion with forearm in non-supinated positions

findings.finding: Measured flexion/extension moment arms of brachioradialis, biceps, brachialis, pronator teres and triceps each changed by at least 30% across a 95-degree elbow range, so leverage depends on elbow angle; the model reproduced these changes. Two specimens only.
findings.locator: Abstract (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 2 anatomic specimens plus a computer model of the elbow

exercises.name: elbow flexion/extension across a 95-degree range of elbow angles

findings.finding: Among 39 competition powerlifters, medium (142% shoulder width) and wide (169%) stance squats produced knee-extensor net moments of 447-756 N·m versus 359-573 N·m for narrow stance (107%); knee moments were greater wide than narrow. Joint demand, not EMG; load normalisation not stated in abstract.
findings.locator: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 39 powerlifters filmed at a national powerlifting championship

findings.finding: Hip-extensor net moments were 382-628 N·m in medium and wide stance squats versus 275-577 N·m in narrow stance, and hip moments were greater wide than narrow; hips flexed 6-11 degrees more with wider stances. Net moment only; glute versus hamstring share not separated.
findings.locator: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 39 powerlifters filmed at a national powerlifting championship

findings.finding: Narrow-stance squats (107% shoulder width) generated a small net ankle plantar-flexor moment (10-51 N·m), whereas medium and wide stances generated net dorsiflexor moments (34-284 N·m), with shanks 5-9 degrees more vertical in wide stance. Net joint moment only; no calf EMG.
findings.locator: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 39 powerlifters filmed at a national powerlifting championship

findings.finding: Twenty women performed one work-matched biceps-curl set at 30%, 60% and 90% 1RM in random order; biceps EMG and RPE rose with intensity (EMG P<0.01), and lactate was higher at 90% than 30%. Acute EMG only; not a growth outcome.
findings.locator: Abstract, Results (full text paywalled; no PMCID, not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 20 women aged 25 +/- 4 yr, single session; training status not given in abstract

findings.finding: Dynamic stretching of five lower-limb muscle groups (500 s total) raised seated leg-extension power from 1837.6±130.8 to 2022.3±121.0 W (mean±SE), increasing in all 11 men; condition-by-time interaction versus no stretching F=35.68, p<0.01. Dynamic versus static was not directly tested.
findings.locator: Results section (author manuscript pp. 8-9), Figure 3; Abstract. Full text read from the Hokkaido University repository copy (HUSCAP hdl 2115/17085) linked by Europe PMC; Tables 1-2 (stretch procedures) are images and could not be read.
findings.population: 11 recreationally active college men (22.8±0.8 y), single sessions on separate days in randomized order

exercises.name: dynamic stretching of lower-limb muscle groups

findings.finding: One 30-s static stretch per muscle group per leg did not significantly alter leg-extension power versus rest: 1884.8→1788.5 W after static, 1851.9→1784.8 W without stretching (mean±SE); interaction F=0.38, p=0.54. Higher baseline power correlated with larger declines (r=-0.71, -0.68).
findings.locator: Results section (author manuscript pp. 8-9), Figure 2 and Figure 3; Abstract
findings.population: 11 recreationally active college men (22.8±0.8 y), single sessions on separate days in randomized order

exercises.name: static stretching 30 s per muscle group

findings.finding: In 13 men, 6-kg shot-put performance correlated with long-head triceps type II fibre area (r=0.70), elbow-extensor isokinetic torque (r=0.65-0.78), one-arm seated shot put (r=0.60-0.79) and estimated arm muscle cross-sectional area (r=0.68). findings.finding: Bench-press maximal-strength (1RM) and explosive bench-throw tests showed the strongest correlations reported with 6-kg shot-put performance (r>0.86, P<0.01); authors infer lower-body contributions also matter. findings.locator: Abstract (full text subscription-only; not in PMC/Europe PMC)
findings.population: 13 male physical-education students tested after 5 weeks of shot-put technique instruction

findings.finding: Analysing numerous training studies, the author estimates that relative intensity (%1RM) accounts for 18-35% of hypertrophy variance and suggests loads of 80-95% 1RM maximise hypertrophy; fibre-type and myosin heavy-chain transitions showed no relation to training intensity.
findings.locator: Abstract (full text subscription-only; not in PMC/Europe PMC); muscles studied not specified in abstract

exercises.name: resistance training at lower relative intensities

findings.finding: Competitive lifters using the heaviest loads (at least 90% 1RM; weightlifters, powerlifters) showed preferential type II fibre hypertrophy, whereas bodybuilders showed roughly equal type I and type II hypertrophy. findings.locator: Abstract (full text subscription-only; not in PMC/Europe PMC)

findings.finding: Restricted to quadriceps and elbow flexors, the review reports that with sufficient frequency, intensity and volume all three muscle-action types examined can yield significant, rapid gains in whole-muscle cross-sectional area; evidence was insufficient to show any mode (dynamic external, accommodating, isometric) or muscle-action type superior.

findings.population: 87 EMG studies of abdominal exercises identified from searches covering 1950-2008

the same abdominal exercises flat and unloaded

sit-ups with internal cues (focus on/feel stomach muscles)
