findings.finding: Cited 12-week Scott-curl trial (3 sets of 8RM): a 4-s eccentric (4/0/1/0) improved strength more than a 1-s eccentric (1/0/1/0); it was the only study isolating eccentric duration and used one single-joint exercise.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Maximal Strength' section, Pereira et al. paragraph
findings.population: 12-week Scott-curl training (cited trial)

findings.finding: Cited 10-week whole-body trial (40-60% 1RM, 8-10 reps): a 1-s concentric (3/0/1/0) gave greater biceps brachii cross-sectional area than a 3-s concentric (3/0/3/0); strength gains were comparable.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Muscle Hypertrophy' section, Nogueira et al. paragraph; 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Maximal Strength' section for comparable strength
findings.population: 10-week whole-body resistance training, 7 exercises (cited trial)

findings.finding: The same cited 10-week trial found no rectus femoris cross-sectional area difference between a 1-s concentric (3/0/1/0) and a 3-s concentric (3/0/3/0) tempo.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Muscle Hypertrophy' section, Nogueira et al. paragraph
findings.population: 10-week whole-body resistance training, 7 exercises (cited trial)

findings.finding: Cited 12-week knee-extension trial (3 sets to failure, 60-s rest): 3/1/3/0 tempo at 50% 1RM gave greater cross-sectional area than 1/1/1/0 at the same load, and growth similar to 1/1/1/0 at 80% 1RM.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Muscle Hypertrophy' section, Tanimoto and Ishii paragraph
findings.population: 12-week knee-extension training (cited trial)

findings.finding: Cited 6-week trial (squat, leg press, leg extension; 3 sets of 6-10RM to failure): 2/0/1/0 tempo at 80-85% 1RM raised mean muscle fibre area more than super-slow 4/0/10/0 at 40-60% 1RM (38.8% vs 10.6%); strength gains did not differ.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Muscle Hypertrophy' section, Schuenke et al. paragraph (biopsy site not stated in review); 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Maximal Strength' section
findings.population: 6-week lower-body training (cited trial)

exercises.name: squat, leg press, leg extension at 2/0/1/0 with 80-85% 1RM
squat, leg press, leg extension at super-slow 4/0/10/0 with 40-60% 1RM

findings.finding: Cited 10-week trial in untrained women (1 set of 8-12 reps to failure, 8 exercises): 4/0/2/0 tempo at 80% 1RM improved strength more than super-slow 5/0/10/0 at 50% 1RM, though not in every exercise; a similar trial found no difference.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Maximal Strength' section, Keeler et al. and Neils et al. paragraph; loads from the hypertrophy section's Keeler et al. sentence
findings.population: untrained women, 10 weeks (cited trial)

findings.finding: Most cited trials changing both phases by 2-3 s found no difference in strength gains over 3-13 weeks in trained and untrained people; the review concludes it is unclear whether any tempo is superior for maximal strength.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Maximal Strength' section, second and third paragraphs; Conclusions
findings.population: trained and untrained adults, 3-13-week programmes

exercises.name: tempo slower by 2-3 s per phase

findings.finding: Cited 8-10-week trial (1 set, 13 exercises): 4/0/10/0 tempo for 4-6 reps raised strength more than 4/0/2/1 for 8-12 reps, but only by 3-4 kg, which the review judges of limited practical relevance.
findings.locator: 'Influence of Movement Tempo on Maximal Strength' section, Westcott et al. paragraph
findings.population: 8-10-week whole-body training, 13 exercises (cited trial)

findings.finding: Cited 8-week within-subject trial in untrained young men: a 20-s loaded inter-set stretch increased soleus thickness more than 2-min passive rest despite 5-12% lower volume load; the gastrocnemius showed no added benefit.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to inter-set stretch', Van Every et al. paragraph
findings.population: untrained young men, 8 weeks (cited trial)

exercises.name: plantar flexion with 20-s loaded inter-set stretch

findings.finding: Cited 8-week total-body trial in untrained young men: a 30-s unloaded stretch to discomfort inside 90-s rests produced larger summed upper- and lower-limb muscle thickness gains than passive rest (10.5% vs 6.7%).
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to inter-set stretch', Evangelista et al. paragraph
findings.population: untrained young men, 8 weeks (cited trial)

exercises.name: total-body resistance training with 30-s unloaded inter-set stretch

findings.finding: Cited 8-week trial in trained men (flat and incline bench press): a 30-s loaded cable-fly stretch between sets gave pectoralis major thickness gains similar to passive rest.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to inter-set stretch', Wadhi et al. paragraph
findings.population: resistance-trained men, 8 weeks (cited trial)

exercises.name: flat and incline bench press with 30-s loaded cable-fly inter-set stretch

findings.finding: The same cited 8-week bench-press trial found similar chest strength gains with and without 30-s loaded inter-set cable-fly stretching; inter-set stretching did not impair strength.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to inter-set stretch', Wadhi et al. paragraph
findings.population: resistance-trained men, 8 weeks (cited trial)

exercises.name: flat and incline bench press with 30-s loaded cable-fly inter-set stretch

findings.finding: Cited trial in untrained young men (flywheel squats twice weekly): adding a 30-s inter-set stretch gave similar quadriceps thickness gains; the review suggests the delay moving to a massage table may have blunted any effect.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to inter-set stretch', Nakamura et al. paragraph
findings.population: untrained young men (cited trial)

findings.finding: In the same cited flywheel-squat trial, strength gains tended to favour adding inter-set stretching. The review gives no statistics or effect sizes and notes that the stretching did not compromise strength.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to inter-set stretch', Nakamura et al. paragraph and Wadhi et al. paragraph (no strength detriment)
findings.population: untrained young men (cited trial)

findings.finding: Cited 10-week trial: two 25-s passive stretches immediately before leg extension attenuated vastus lateralis cross-sectional area gains versus training alone (7.4% vs 12.7%), associated with fewer repetitions performed.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to longitudinal isolated stretch protocols', Junior et al. sentence
findings.population: 10-week leg-extension training (cited trial)

exercises.name: passive stretching immediately before leg extension

findings.finding: Cited 6-week trial in healthy men: 360 s per week of static plantar-flexor stretching, in one or three sessions, did not change medial gastrocnemius thickness; a follow-up with two 30-min weekly sessions also showed no plantar-flexor hypertrophy.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to longitudinal isolated stretch protocols', Sato et al. paragraph
findings.population: healthy men, 6 weeks (cited trials)

exercises.name: static plantar-flexor stretching 360 s per week in one session
static plantar-flexor stretching 360 s per week over three sessions

findings.finding: Cited 6-week trial: stretching the calves with an orthosis for 1 h daily at discomfort 8/10 increased lateral gastrocnemius thickness by about 15%; the review judges this dose impractical for most people.
findings.locator: Section 'Hypertrophic adaptations to longitudinal isolated stretch protocols', Warneke et al. sentence
findings.population: free-living adults, 6 weeks (cited trial)

findings.finding: Review concludes inter-set stretching may enhance hypertrophy without lengthening sessions, apparently when done immediately after a set's last repetition; evidence is preliminary, limited to young men, and shows no long-term strength detriment.
findings.population: young men (all studies to date)

exercises.name: resistance training with inter-set stretch immediately after each set
resistance training with passive inter-set rest

findings.finding: Review of 10 human studies: 3 found positive muscle-structure effects of stretch training, all using an apparatus or external load; passive stretching at self-determined range showed no effect on muscle size or architecture.
findings.population: 10 human stretch-training studies

exercises.name: passive low-intensity stretching at self-determined range of motion

findings.finding: Of 5 studies combining stretching with resistance training, the 2 placing stretching in the inter-set rest period showed enhanced muscle growth; the authors describe this evidence as limited.
findings.population: 5 human studies combining stretching with resistance training

exercises.name: resistance training with stretching in the inter-set rest period
resistance training with stretching at other times

findings.finding: In 83 trained men, ultrasound pectoralis major thickness correlated r = 0.83 with barbell bench-press 1RM; thickness alone explained R² = 0.69 (RMSE 12.89 kg), plus body mass R² = 0.76 (RMSE 11.33 kg; abstract says 0.79). Correlational; no exercise comparison.
findings.locator: Results section (author accepted manuscript, IRIS Università di Bologna, hdl 11585/1001171); Abstract
findings.population: 83 resistance-trained men (>=3 y training), single testing visit

findings.finding: In this 11-study review, full ROM and initial-portion (lengthened) partial ROM each outgrew final-portion (shortened) partial ROM for rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, biceps brachii and brachialis at distal sites, per abstract wording (between-group ES 0.20–0.90; a range, not pooled).
findings.population: 11 training studies comparing full vs partial ROM (literature to April 2022)

exercises.name: partial range of motion, initial (lengthened) portion
partial range of motion, final (shortened) portion

findings.finding: Full ROM produced greater gluteus maximus and adductor hypertrophy than partial ROM confined to the final (shortened) portion of the movement (between-group ES 0.24–0.25).
findings.population: 11 training studies comparing full vs partial ROM (literature to April 2022)

exercises.name: partial range of motion, final (shortened) portion

findings.finding: Partial ROM in the initial (lengthened) portion produced more proximal rectus femoris hypertrophy than full ROM (between-group ES 0.35–0.38).
findings.population: 11 training studies comparing full vs partial ROM (literature to April 2022)

exercises.name: partial range of motion, initial (lengthened) portion

findings.finding: Partial ROM through the middle portion of the movement yielded more triceps brachii growth than full ROM (between-group ES 1.21); how many included studies underlie this estimate could not be checked without the full text.
findings.population: 11 training studies comparing full vs partial ROM (literature to April 2022)

exercises.name: partial range of motion, middle portion

findings.finding: In 23 trained adults (6 wk, twice weekly unilateral knee extension), long-length isometric and full-ROM isotonic training gave similar quadriceps growth: summed anterior-thigh difference −0.20 cm (HDI −0.54 to 0.16); proximal site −0.11 cm (95% HDI −0.24 to 0.02), leaning isometric, uncertain.
findings.population: 23 resistance-trained men and women, 6 weeks, 2 sessions/week

exercises.name: isometric knee extension at long muscle length
full range of motion isotonic knee extension

findings.finding: MRI after 12 weeks (5×10 at 70% 1RM, twice weekly): rectus femoris volume rose 13.2% with knee extension but only 1.1% (non-significant, P=0.379) with leg press; between-condition difference P<0.001.
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Vasti gains were similar for knee extension and leg press (vastus lateralis 6.4% vs 6.2%, medialis 7.2% vs 6.0%, intermedius 5.0% vs 4.4%); whole quadriceps 7.1% vs 4.9%, no significant interaction (P≥0.319).
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Leg press increased gluteus maximus volume 15.4% (whole gluteal group 12.0%) while knee extension produced no change (about +0.2%); between-condition difference P<0.001. Gluteus medius and minimus did not change significantly with either exercise.
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Leg press increased adductor magnus volume 6.2% and the adductor group 4.1%, whereas knee extension did not (about −0.9%); between-condition difference P<0.001. Adductor longus, adductor brevis, pectineus and gracilis were unchanged with both.
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Hamstrings grew only slightly with both (group 1.5% knee extension vs 3.1% leg press; biceps femoris long head 2.0% vs 5.3%), no between-condition difference; authors judge neither exercise an effective primary hamstring builder.
findings.locator: Results, Experiment 1; Table 1; Discussion (Other lower-limb muscles)
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Summed volume of 17 hip and thigh muscles rose 6.3% after leg press versus 2.8% after knee extension (difference P<0.001), so leg press was the more time-efficient option for overall lower-limb muscle mass in untrained adults.
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Unilateral knee-extension 1RM rose 22.4 kg after knee-extension training versus 8.5 kg after leg-press training (P<0.001); its change correlated very strongly with quadriceps volume change (r = 0.820) but not with other muscle groups.
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Unilateral leg-press 1RM rose 69.7 kg after leg-press training versus 35.7 kg after knee-extension training (P<0.001); its change correlated with quadriceps, gluteal, hamstring and adductor volume changes (r = 0.63–0.77).
findings.population: 17 untrained young adults (11 men, 6 women), 12 weeks

findings.finding: At 50% 1RM, rectus femoris excitation was higher during knee extension than leg press (38.0% vs 21.7% EMGmax, P<0.001). EMG amplitude only, not a growth outcome.
findings.population: 11 healthy men, single session, 10 reps at 50% 1RM

findings.finding: At 50% 1RM, vasti excitation did not differ between knee extension and leg press (vastus lateralis 36.9% vs 37.1%, P=0.944; vastus medialis 32.4% vs 35.0% EMGmax, P=0.653).
findings.population: 11 healthy men, single session, 10 reps at 50% 1RM

findings.finding: At 50% 1RM, gluteus maximus excitation was far greater during leg press than knee extension (41.2% vs 8.8% EMGmax, P<0.001).
findings.population: 11 healthy men, single session, 10 reps at 50% 1RM

findings.finding: At 50% 1RM, hamstring excitation was higher during leg press than knee extension (biceps femoris long head 13.9% vs 7.3%, P=0.004; semitendinosus 18.9% vs 8.1% EMGmax, P=0.005), though low in both.
findings.population: 11 healthy men, single session, 10 reps at 50% 1RM

findings.finding: With matched resistance profiles and elbow ROM, cable curls at peak shoulder extension versus neutral gave similar elbow-flexor thickness gains (distal 7.2% vs 6.3%, proximal 7.9% vs 9.2%); ATE proximal −0.40 mm, distal 0.21 mm; BF 0.56 and 0.24 favouring null.
findings.population: 24 untrained men analysed (30 randomized), 10 weeks, 6–8 weekly sets to failure

exercises.name: cable curl with shoulder at individual peak extension (~43°)
cable curl with shoulder in neutral

findings.finding: Over 10 weeks at matched relative load, full-ROM bench press improved most on all three bench ROM tests (ES 0.52-1.96) vs two-thirds (0.29-0.78) and one-third ROM (-0.01 to 0.66). These within-group ESs are not split by 1RM vs velocity; no between-group statistics given.
findings.population: 50 recreationally to highly resistance-trained men, 10 weeks

exercises.name: full range of motion bench press
two-thirds range of motion bench press
one-third range of motion bench press

findings.finding: Load-matched push-ups and 40%1RM bench press gave similar ultrasound thickness gains (push-up vs bench: pectoralis +18.3% vs +19.4%, triceps +9.5% vs +10.3%); no between-group difference. Reported means disagree (identical pectoral values across groups; bench triceps means imply about +6%), so magnitudes are unreliable.
findings.population: 18 male PE students with at least 1 year of recreational resistance training, 8 weeks

findings.finding: Biceps thickness rose only with bench press (28.4 to 31.5 mm, p<0.01), not with push-ups (29.3 to 30.3 mm, p=0.315); groups did not differ significantly. The authors offer grip width as a possible but, in their words, unlikely explanation.
findings.population: 18 male PE students with at least 1 year of recreational resistance training, 8 weeks

findings.finding: Bench press 1RM rose in both groups: bench 60.0 to 65.0 kg (about 8%), push-up 61.1 to 64.2 kg (about 5%), both p<0.01 within group. The authors call the gains comparable; the text gives no between-group 1RM statistic.
findings.population: 18 male PE students with at least 1 year of recreational resistance training, 8 weeks

findings.finding: Reps to failure at 40%1RM on the bench press did not change significantly within either group. The percent change still differed between groups (p<0.01) in favour of bench-press training, which the authors attribute to test specificity.
findings.population: 18 male PE students with at least 1 year of recreational resistance training, 8 weeks

findings.finding: Kneeling medicine-ball throw (2 and 4 kg) did not improve in either group and did not differ between groups after 8 weeks of controlled-tempo low-load training.
findings.population: 18 male PE students with at least 1 year of recreational resistance training, 8 weeks

findings.finding: Over 5 weeks, 6RM bench press and 6RM elastic-band push-up groups both significantly improved 1RM and 6RM with similar gains (changes 13.65-22.21%); controls were unchanged. The three-group comparison of percent change was significant (6RM p=0.017; 1RM p<0.001).
findings.population: 30 university students with advanced resistance-training experience, 5 weeks

findings.finding: Within subjects, 1 vs 3 sets of pec deck to failure over 12 weeks produced similar ultrasound pectoralis thickness gains: clavicular +17% vs +18%, sternocostal +21% vs +21%.
findings.population: 15 untrained young men, 12 weeks

findings.finding: With pec deck training, clavicular thickness rose 17-18% and sternocostal thickness 21% (across both volume conditions). The authors conclude their data do not support region-specific pectoral hypertrophy in untrained men; the abstract reports no between-region statistic.
findings.population: 15 untrained young men, 12 weeks

findings.finding: Pec deck 1RM increased similarly with 1 set (+46%) and 3 sets (+43%) per session over 12 weeks.
findings.population: 15 untrained young men, 12 weeks

findings.finding: Across 16 RCTs (n=551), full-ROM training increased strength more than partial ROM (ES 0.56, 95% CI 0.20-0.91, p=0.004; I2 77.6%). Exercises included squat, bench press, elbow flexion/extension, knee extension/flexion, leg press, lumbar extension and arm push-pull.
findings.population: 551 healthy adults in 16 RCTs (10 male-only, 2 female-only, 4 mixed samples; untrained to highly trained), 6-16 weeks

exercises.name: full range of motion resistance training
partial range of motion resistance training

findings.finding: Lower-limb 1RM tested at full ROM improved more after full-ROM training (ES 1.53, 0.94-2.11, p=0.001; 6 RCTs, 127 participants; GRADE moderate). When tested at partial ROM there was no difference (ES -0.27, -1.03 to 0.50, p=0.412).
findings.population: 127 adults in 6 RCTs, mostly squat training

findings.finding: Upper-limb 1RM tested at full ROM (4 RCTs, 101 participants; bench press and elbow flexion) favoured full ROM but not significantly (ES 0.69, -0.14 to 1.52, p=0.078; GRADE moderate). Upper-limb isokinetic strength: ES 0.24, p=0.424 (2 RCTs).
findings.population: 101 adults in 4 RCTs (three bench press trials, one elbow flexion trial)

exercises.name: full range of motion bench press / elbow flexion
partial range of motion bench press / elbow flexion

findings.finding: Full-ROM lower-limb training produced more hypertrophy (MRI or ultrasound CSA/volume) than partial ROM (ES 0.88, 95% CI 0.19-1.57, p=0.027; I2 80.3%; 4 studies using squat, knee extension or knee flexion).
findings.population: 4 RCTs of lower-limb training in adults

exercises.name: full range of motion squat / knee extension / knee flexion
partial range of motion squat / knee extension / knee flexion

findings.finding: Upper-limb hypertrophy was not meta-analysed: the only upper-limb size study was one elbow-extension trial measuring triceps CSA at a single site, and the authors say evidence is too scarce to conclude how ROM affects upper-limb growth.

exercises.name: full range of motion upper-limb exercise
partial range of motion upper-limb exercise

findings.finding: Pooled muscle thickness (3 RCTs: squat, elbow flexion, leg press) showed no ROM difference (ES 0.05, -0.30 to 0.39, p=0.605, I2 0%). Overall architecture, which also covers pennation and fascicle length, was not significant (ES 0.28, p=0.226).
findings.population: 76 adults in 3 RCTs

exercises.name: full range of motion resistance training
partial range of motion resistance training

findings.finding: Jump-height gains favoured full ROM without reaching significance (ES 0.55, -0.41 to 1.51, p=0.164; 4 RCTs, 98 participants). Sprint results were inconclusive (ES 0.10, p=0.923; 2 RCTs), and overall functional performance was ES 0.44, p=0.186.
findings.population: 98 adults in 4 RCTs, mostly squat training

findings.finding: Clavicular (upper) pectoralis EMG did not differ between 0, 15, 30 and 45 degrees (roughly 25-30% MVIC; 0 vs 30 degrees p=0.688) and was significantly lower at 60 degrees (under 20%; p<=0.002). Pairwise tests do not support the abstract's claimed 30-degree advantage over flat.
findings.population: 30 resistance-trained adults (at least 1 year), single session

findings.finding: Sternal (middle) and costal (lower) pectoralis EMG was highest on the flat bench (about 27% MVIC) and fell significantly with each step up in incline (all pairwise p<=0.016).
findings.population: 30 resistance-trained adults (at least 1 year), single session

findings.finding: Anterior deltoid EMG rose with incline (about 26% MVIC flat to about 33%). Compared with flat, it was higher at 30 (p=0.014), 45 (p=0.001) and 60 degrees (p<0.001) but not 15 degrees (p=0.170); 30, 45 and 60 degrees did not differ from each other.
findings.population: 30 resistance-trained adults (at least 1 year), single session

findings.finding: Triceps medial-head EMG stayed at about 15% MVIC at every bench angle, with no pairwise differences (all p=1.000).
findings.population: 30 resistance-trained adults (at least 1 year), single session

findings.finding: Upper (clavicular) pectoralis: moving from flat to 45-degree incline shifted the barycentre of EMG amplitude toward the clavicular region (p<0.001). Number and spread of active channels, range of motion and cycle duration did not differ. Regional distribution shift, not total amplitude.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed record); full text not accessed
findings.population: 8 volunteers (sex and training status not stated in abstract); acute; flat vs 45-degree incline bench at 50% and 70% 1RM

findings.finding: Sternocostal (mid/lower) pectoralis: in the flat bench press the largest EMG amplitudes were concentrated over the sternocostal head, whereas the incline centred them on the clavicular head. Relative distribution only; absolute regional amplitudes not reported in the abstract.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed record); full text not accessed
findings.population: 8 volunteers (sex and training status not stated in abstract); acute; flat vs 45-degree incline bench at 50% and 70% 1RM

findings.finding: Anterior deltoid: shoulder press reached 33.3% MVIC, significantly above bench press 21.4%, lateral raise 21.2% and dumbbell fly 18.8% (ES 1.14-1.41, moderate); bench press, lateral raise and fly did not differ from one another.

findings.finding: Medial deltoid: lateral raise 30.3% MVIC and shoulder press 27.9% did not differ (p=0.596, ES 0.22), and both far exceeded bench press 5.0% and dumbbell fly 3.4% (ES 2.68-3.48, large).
findings.population: 13 resistance-trained men (3.6 +/- 2.9 y experience); acute; 1 set x 12 reps at 60% 1RM, 2-0-1-0 tempo

findings.finding: Posterior deltoid: lateral raise 24.0% MVIC exceeded shoulder press 11.4% (ES 2.12), which exceeded bench press 3.5% and dumbbell fly 2.5% (ES 2.73-3.43). Reverse fly and rows, the usual rear-deltoid choices, were not tested.
findings.population: 13 resistance-trained men (3.6 +/- 2.9 y experience); acute; 1 set x 12 reps at 60% 1RM, 2-0-1-0 tempo

lateral raise with elbow flexed 90 degrees

findings.finding: Medial deltoid (ascending): behind-neck barbell press exceeded front barbell (ES 3.68) and behind-neck machine (7.51); front barbell exceeded front machine (2.25); behind-neck machine exceeded front machine (1.81). Descending phase showed the same ranking.
findings.population: 8 male competitive bodybuilders; acute; seated presses, 6 reps at 80% 1RM, 2 s up / 2 s down

findings.finding: Posterior deltoid (ascending): behind-neck barbell press exceeded front barbell (ES 9.00) and behind-neck machine (4.09); behind-neck machine exceeded front machine (4.42); front barbell exceeded front machine (2.08). Descending phase similar (ES up to 8.65).
findings.population: 8 male competitive bodybuilders; acute; seated presses, 6 reps at 80% 1RM, 2 s up / 2 s down

findings.finding: Anterior deltoid: ascending, behind-neck barbell press beat front and behind-neck machine presses (ES 2.80, 1.42) but not front barbell; descending, it beat front barbell (7.66) and behind-neck machine (3.26). The paper's Conclusion claims no anterior-deltoid difference, contradicting its Results.
findings.population: 8 male competitive bodybuilders; acute; seated presses, 6 reps at 80% 1RM, 2 s up / 2 s down

findings.finding: Upper trapezius: no between-exercise difference among front barbell, behind-neck barbell, front machine and behind-neck machine presses in either the ascending or descending phase (no load x position x phase interaction).
findings.population: 8 male competitive bodybuilders; acute; seated presses, 6 reps at 80% 1RM, 2 s up / 2 s down

findings.finding: Clavicular pectoralis major: front variants exceeded their behind-neck counterparts, barbell (ascending ES 3.11; descending 4.20) and machine (ascending ES 20.52; descending 7.03).
findings.population: 8 male competitive bodybuilders; acute; seated presses, 6 reps at 80% 1RM, 2 s up / 2 s down

findings.finding: Lateral triceps head: no difference among the four presses in the ascending phase; in the descending phase front barbell exceeded behind-neck barbell (ES 8.29) and front machine (3.48), and front machine exceeded behind-neck machine (1.55).
findings.population: 8 male competitive bodybuilders; acute; seated presses, 6 reps at 80% 1RM, 2 s up / 2 s down

findings.finding: Stopping pull-up sets at 25% velocity loss gave significantly larger gains than 50% in estimated 1RM, mean velocity against common loads, peak bodyweight velocity and velocity at matched reps; 25% group improved on all (p<0.001), 50% group unchanged. Muscles not measured.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed record); full text not accessed
findings.population: 29 strength-trained men (baseline 15.9 +/- 4.9 pull-ups to failure), 8 weeks (16 sessions)

exercises.name: bodyweight prone-grip pull-up, sets stopped at 25% velocity loss
bodyweight prone-grip pull-up, sets stopped at 50% velocity loss

findings.finding: Maximum bodyweight pull-up reps to failure improved significantly within the 25% velocity-loss group (p<0.001) while the 50% group did not change, but the between-group difference for this outcome was not statistically significant.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed record); full text not accessed
findings.population: 29 strength-trained men (baseline 15.9 +/- 4.9 pull-ups to failure), 8 weeks (16 sessions)

exercises.name: bodyweight prone-grip pull-up, sets stopped at 25% velocity loss
bodyweight prone-grip pull-up, sets stopped at 50% velocity loss

findings.finding: The programme reduced forward head angle and forward shoulder translation relative to control (significant group-by-time interactions, p<0.05). The abstract gives no effect magnitudes and does not list the exercises, so exercise content and targeted muscles are unverified.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed record); full text not accessed
findings.population: 28 NCAA Division I varsity swimmers, 8 weeks

findings.finding: Hand-held dynamometer strength of all shoulder-girdle muscle groups tested rose over time (main effect of time, p<0.05); the abstract does not report a group-by-time interaction, so strength gains cannot be attributed to the programme over control.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed record); full text not accessed
findings.population: 28 NCAA Division I varsity swimmers, 8 weeks

findings.finding: Mid-arm biceps thickness grew by a similar amount with cable preacher curl (25 to 27 mm, +7%, ES 0.37) and barbell preacher curl (24 to 26 mm, +8%, ES 0.35); between-group p=0.346. The programme also included a wide-grip lat pulldown.
findings.locator: Results section (biceps thickness paragraph); Abstract; Discussion limitations
findings.population: 35 untrained young adults (25 men, 10 women), 3 sessions/week, 3x8-12 near failure, 10 weeks

findings.finding: Isokinetic elbow-flexion torque rose in both groups. The barbell group gained more only near full extension (20 deg: +39% vs +30%, p=0.046, small ES 0.23). Gains at 60 deg (+32% vs +27%, p=0.874) and 100 deg (+20% vs +17%, p=0.728) were similar.
findings.locator: Results section (peak torque paragraph); Discussion first paragraph (ES 0.23); Abstract reports the barbell 100 deg gain as 19%
findings.population: 35 untrained young adults (25 men, 10 women), 10 weeks

findings.finding: Over the whole rep, biceps EMG was higher for EZ-bar curl than alternating dumbbell curl (p<0.05, ES 0.30), with no EZ vs straight-bar difference. In the eccentric phase EZ (ES 0.45) and straight bar (ES 0.28) beat dumbbell. Concentric: no significant differences.
findings.population: 12 resistance-trained men (3+ years), one set of 10 reps at 65% 1RM per variant, single session; no MVC normalisation reported

findings.finding: Brachioradialis EMG was higher for EZ-bar curl than alternating dumbbell curl over the whole rep (p<0.01, ES 0.51), in the concentric phase (p<0.001, ES 0.48) and in the eccentric phase (p<0.01, ES 0.66). Straight-bar curl beat dumbbell only in the concentric phase (p<0.05, ES 0.36).
findings.population: 12 resistance-trained men (3+ years), 65% 1RM, single session

findings.finding: Brachioradialis sEMG (normalised to MVC in each hand position) was significantly higher with the hand pronated than neutral or supinated, across 0-120 deg and in every 25 deg interval (p<0.05). Neutral and supinated did not differ (p=0.67). Slow 20 deg/s movements; no external load reported.
findings.locator: Results section; Figures 2-3; Methods (study protocol, MVC normalisation)
findings.population: 16 healthy adults (12 men, 4 women), single session, 20 reps per hand position

findings.finding: Biceps brachii sEMG, normalised to MVC in the matching hand position, did not differ between pronated, neutral and supinated elbow flexion (p=0.63). Because each position had its own normalisation, absolute biceps activity was not compared across grips.
findings.locator: Results section; Methods (Normalization via MVC); Discussion (normalisation caveat)
findings.population: 16 healthy adults (12 men, 4 women), single session

findings.finding: Front lat pulldown gave more concentric lat EMG than behind-the-neck pulldown in 24 trained men (Sperandei 2009) and in an HD-sEMG study of 14 (Padovan 2024). In the second study, behind-the-neck showed more lat excitation in the eccentric phase.
findings.population: 24 trained men + 14 resistance-trained men (two acute EMG studies)

findings.finding: Behind-the-neck pulldown drew more posterior deltoid and biceps EMG than front pulldown, which drew more pectoralis major and lat EMG concentrically (Sperandei 2009, 24 trained men, as summarised by the review).
findings.population: 24 trained men, single-session EMG

findings.finding: Pulldown grip width had no consistent effect on lat EMG. An early 10-man study favoured a wide front grip, but studies of 15 men (Andersen 2014) and 40 trained men (Buonsenso 2025) found no grip-width differences.
findings.population: 10 healthy men; 15 men; 40 resistance-trained men (three acute EMG studies)

findings.finding: Pronated-grip lat pulldown gave more lat EMG than supinated-grip pulldown in 12 healthy men (Lusk 2010). The review notes this result has not been replicated.
findings.population: 12 healthy men, single-session EMG

findings.finding: Supinated-grip pulldown drew more biceps EMG than pronated grip (Lusk 2010, 12 men). Medium or narrow pulldown grips drew more biceps EMG whatever the forearm orientation (Andersen 2014, 15 men).
findings.population: 12 healthy men; 15 men (two acute EMG studies)

findings.finding: Of the pulldown variants tested at 70% 1RM in 40 trained men (Buonsenso 2025), only a ~30 deg backward trunk lean with a wide pronated grip significantly raised posterior deltoid EMG. Lat EMG was unchanged.
findings.population: 40 resistance-trained men (5+ years), 70% 1RM

exercises.name: lat pulldown with ~30 deg backward lean, wide pronated grip

findings.finding: The pullover is not lat-selective: it drew more pectoralis major than lat EMG (8 men). Isometric lat EMG was broadly comparable to the pulldown across shoulder angles (15 men). Versus straight-arm pulldown (20 adults), barbell pullover raised most muscles' EMG except lats and triceps.
findings.population: 8 healthy men; 15 recreationally trained men (isometric); 20 physically active adults

findings.finding: In an HD-sEMG study of 14 trained men (Padovan 2025), narrow-grip seated row gave more lat EMG than wide grip in both concentric and eccentric phases (ES 1.08). The review says this applies to the seated row only.
findings.population: 14 resistance-trained men

findings.finding: Compared with narrow grip, wide-grip seated row raised EMG in upper trapezius (ES 1.35 concentric / 2.79 eccentric), middle trapezius (1.24/1.44), lower trapezius (0.90/0.71) and lateral deltoid (1.03/0.58), plus erector spinae in the eccentric phase only (0.65). Source: Padovan 2025, 14 trained men.
findings.population: 14 resistance-trained men

findings.finding: In 21 recreationally trained adults (de Abreu Vasconcelos 2023), seated cable rows with lower shoulder-abduction angles favoured lat EMG in both dynamic and isometric tests. Low abduction has not been tested together with a narrow grip.
findings.population: 11 recreationally trained men and 10 women

exercises.name: seated cable row, low shoulder abduction
seated cable row, 60-90 deg shoulder abduction

findings.finding: Seated cable rows at 60 and 90 deg shoulder abduction raised upper and middle trapezius and posterior deltoid EMG compared with lower abduction angles (de Abreu Vasconcelos 2023; 11 men, 10 women).
findings.population: 11 recreationally trained men and 10 women

exercises.name: seated cable row, 60-90 deg shoulder abduction
seated cable row, low shoulder abduction

findings.finding: Deliberate scapular retraction during the seated row (12 trained men, 10-12RM; Lehman 2004) did not raise middle trapezius or rhomboid EMG and did not change lat EMG. The review notes that testing was isometric only.
findings.population: 12 healthy men with 6+ months resistance training

exercises.name: seated row with active scapular retraction

findings.finding: In an HD-sEMG study of 14 trained men (Padovan 2026), fixed- and free-scapula seated rows were broadly similar. Fixing the scapula raised posterior deltoid EMG in the concentric phase and middle trapezius and lat EMG in the eccentric phase.
findings.population: 14 resistance-trained men (age 25 +/- 4)

findings.finding: In 7 men (Fenwick 2009), the inverted row gave the highest lat and upper-back EMG and the lowest lumbar load, compared with the standing bent-over row and the standing one-arm cable row. The review rates this preliminary (lowest quality band).
findings.population: 7 healthy university men

findings.finding: In the prone barbell row at 10RM (16 trained men; Fischer 2025), mean lat excitation was higher with upper-half partial reps than with lower-half (p<0.001, ES 0.59) or full-range reps (p<0.001, ES 0.58). Posterior deltoid and biceps were unaffected.
findings.population: 16 resistance-trained men, 10RM

exercises.name: prone barbell row, upper-half range of motion
prone barbell row, lower-half range of motion
prone barbell row, full range of motion

findings.finding: In the same prone-row study, peak excitation of the transverse (middle) trapezius was lower with upper-half reps than with lower-half (p=0.042, ES 0.42) or full-range reps (p=0.013, ES 0.54).
findings.population: 16 resistance-trained men, 10RM

exercises.name: prone barbell row, lower-half range of motion
prone barbell row, full range of motion
prone barbell row, upper-half range of motion

findings.finding: In the bent-over row at 60% 1RM (20 active male students; Swann & Barry 2025), a wide grip (150% of biacromial width) gave more mean lat EMG than a narrow grip (100%). Single unreplicated study; within-subject variability between limbs and across repetitions was noted.
findings.population: 20 active male university students, 60% 1RM

findings.finding: In a preliminary study of 3 trained students (Garcia-Jaen 2021), bench-supported rows showed lower lumbar and thoracic erector EMG than the standing bent-over row. No comparison between conditions was statistically significant.
findings.population: 3 young resistance-trained university students

findings.finding: The supinated-grip chin-up drew more biceps and pectoralis major EMG than the pronated-grip pull-up in 25 adults (21 men, 4 women; Youdas 2010).
findings.population: 21 men and 4 women

findings.finding: The pronated-grip pull-up was linked to relatively higher lower-trapezius EMG than the supinated chin-up (Youdas 2010, 25 adults).
findings.population: 21 men and 4 women

findings.finding: The review rates lat EMG as broadly similar across pull-up and chin-up grips, citing four studies (n about 84). Its text gives direct support from 19 strength-trained men (pronated, supinated, neutral, rope grips); a 10-man study found wider pronated grips slightly lowered lat EMG.
findings.population: Four acute EMG studies, mostly men (combined n about 84: 25, 10, 19, 30)

findings.finding: In 30 strength-trained men (Escalante 2015), grip-assist devices (Versa Grips) reduced wrist flexor and extensor EMG without meaningfully changing lat or infraspinatus EMG.
findings.population: 30 healthy strength-trained men

findings.finding: Back squat grew quadriceps thickness more than hip thrust (+12.2% vs +2%, p<0.001). Read from the abstract only. A 2020 white paper flagged improbable data from this lab and asked for this paper's retraction; PubMed did not show it as retracted when checked.
findings.population: 22 well-trained women (12 back squat, 10 hip thrust), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Back squat grew gluteus maximus thickness more than hip thrust (+9.4% vs +3.7%, p=0.001). Read from the abstract only. A 2020 white paper raised data-integrity concerns, and four other papers by this first author are marked retracted in PubMed.
findings.population: 22 well-trained women (12 back squat, 10 hip thrust), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Back-squat 1RM rose 35.9% with squat training vs 4.3% with hip-thrust training (p<0.001). Hip-thrust 1RM rose by a similar amount in both groups (figures not given in the abstract). Read from the abstract only; data-integrity concerns have been raised.
findings.population: 22 well-trained women (12 back squat, 10 hip thrust), 12 weeks

findings.finding: Full-squat training raised Smith-machine 1RM at all three depths (full 82.7 to 96.3 kg, ES 1.22; parallel ES 1.13; half ES 0.77). The parallel group came second (ES 0.58-0.88). The half-squat group had no significant gains (ES 0.21-0.48) and more pain and stiffness.
findings.locator: Submitted manuscript (Univ. Granada DIGIBUG repository, handle 10481/99167): Results; Tables 2 and 4. The published abstract's ES ranges pool 1RM with velocity/functional outcomes and differ from these 1RM-only ranges
findings.population: 53 resistance-trained men randomised (50 analysed), 2 sessions/week velocity-based Smith-machine training at 60-80% 1RM, 10 weeks

findings.finding: Jump and sprint gains grew with squat depth. CMJ rose significantly only after full squats (35.8 to 40.4 cm, ES 0.85); parallel ES 0.56, half 0.28. 20-m sprint: full -2.4% (ES 0.48), parallel -1.0% (ES 0.30), half unchanged. Wingate peak power ES 0.35, 0.15, -0.11.
findings.locator: Submitted manuscript (Univ. Granada DIGIBUG repository, handle 10481/99167): Results; Table 3
findings.population: 53 resistance-trained men randomised (50 analysed), 10 weeks

findings.finding: Pooled mean gluteus maximus EMG was highest for loaded step-up variants (125.09% MVIC), then hip thrusts (75.41%, 5 studies), deadlifts (61.02%, 4), back squats (53.10%, 10) and front squat (40.54%, 2). Step-up data came from one 15-person study; normalisation methods varied.
findings.population: 16 studies, 231 trained adults (90 women, 141 men); loads 40-100% 1RM or 3-12RM

findings.finding: In one 15-person study at 6RM, the forward step-up produced higher gluteus maximus EMG (169.22% MVIC) than lateral (114.25%), diagonal (113.21%) and crossover step-ups (104.19%); reviewers warn the stability demand of step-ups may cap usable load.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Simenz et al. 2012 row); Table 3; Discussion paragraph 2
findings.population: Single included study, 15 resistance-trained women, 6RM loads

findings.finding: Single studies found higher gluteus maximus EMG in the back squat than the overhead squat at 60-90% 3RM and than the belt squat at 5RM; the review's pooled averages (overhead 39.75%, belt 71.34%, back 53.10% MVIC) mix different studies.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Aspe and Swinton 2014; Evans et al. rows); Table 2
findings.population: Two included studies (14 and 31 trained participants)

findings.finding: Two studies (10RM and 1RM loads) found no difference in gluteus maximus EMG between front and back squats; one of them also found none between parallel and full-depth back squats.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Contreras et al. and Yavuz et al. 2015 rows); Discussion paragraph 3
findings.population: Two included studies, 38 trained participants

findings.finding: In one study of 18 resistance-trained women, with EMG recorded at 8RM loads for all lifts, the modified single-leg squat produced greater gluteus maximus EMG (65.6% MVIC) than the bilateral squat (40.3%) and stiff-leg deadlift (40.5%).
findings.locator: Table 1 (McCurdy et al. row); Tables 2-3; McCurdy et al. 2018 primary abstract (PMID 29076958)
findings.population: Single included study, 18 resistance-trained young women, 8RM loads during EMG

findings.finding: Sumo and conventional deadlifts did not differ in gluteus maximus EMG in the included 12RM comparison (Escamilla et al. 2002).
findings.population: Single included study, 13 collegiate football players, 12RM

findings.finding: With load matched to each depth (10RM), partial (0-90 degree) back squats produced higher gluteus maximus EMG than full (0-140 degree) squats in one study; reviewers note training studies still favour deeper squats for muscle and functional gains.
findings.locator: Table 1 (Da Silva et al. 2017 row); Discussion paragraph 3
findings.population: Single included study, 15 resistance-trained men, 10RM per depth

findings.finding: In-line and traditional lunges produced similar gluteus maximus EMG at 10RM (67% vs 66% MVIC) in one 15-person study.
findings.population: Single included study, 15 resistance-trained men, 10RM

findings.finding: Hip thrust gluteus maximus EMG exceeded the back squat (upper/lower means 69%/87% vs 29%/45% MVIC; 13 women), back and split squats (105% vs 69%; 12 men) and hex-bar deadlift (upper lift half 108% vs 85%; 13 men), but not the conventional deadlift (95%).
findings.locator: Results, Muscle activation; Tables 1-2; cross-checked with Andersen et al. 2018 accepted manuscript Results
findings.population: Three acute EMG studies of trained adults (13 women; 12 men; 13 men)

findings.finding: In 13 trained women, biceps femoris EMG was higher during the barbell hip thrust than the back squat (mean 41% vs 15% MVIC; peak 87% vs 37%).
findings.locator: Table 2 (Contreras et al. 2015 row); Results text after Table 2
findings.population: 13 trained women, single acute session, estimated 10RM

findings.finding: In 13 trained men at 1RM, the conventional deadlift gave higher biceps femoris EMG than the hip thrust over the whole lift (+20%) and its lower half (100% vs 68% MVIC); the upper half showed no reported difference (115% vs 110%). Hex-bar: 85% lower, 80% upper.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Andersen et al. 2018 row); Results text after Table 2; Andersen et al. 2018 accepted manuscript Results
findings.population: 13 resistance-trained men, 1RM loads

findings.finding: Erector spinae EMG did not differ between barbell hip thrust, conventional deadlift and hex-bar deadlift in 13 trained men at 1RM (upper half of lift 93%, 88%, 83%; lower half 83%, 90%, 85% MVIC).
findings.locator: Table 1 and Table 2 (Andersen et al. 2018 rows); Results; Andersen et al. 2018 accepted manuscript Results
findings.population: 13 resistance-trained men, 1RM loads

findings.finding: Vastus lateralis EMG did not differ significantly between barbell hip thrust and back squat in 13 women (mean 99% vs 110% MVIC; peak 216% vs 244%); the review relays the original authors' statistical caveat and still hypothesises squats load the quadriceps more.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Contreras et al. 2015 row); Discussion paragraph 4
findings.population: 13 trained women, single acute session, estimated 10RM

findings.finding: The full-range traditional barbell hip thrust gave higher upper gluteus maximus EMG than the American (shorter range, posterior pelvic tilt) and band-resisted versions (mean 69% vs 57% vs 49% MVIC); lower gluteus maximus was similar (87%, 90%, 79%).
findings.locator: Results, Muscle activation; Table 2 (Contreras et al. 2016 row)
findings.population: 13 trained women, 10RM loads

findings.finding: In 7 experienced men at 40% 1RM, a hip thrust performed while deliberately pushing into hip external rotation produced higher gluteus maximus EMG than the standard version (mean 86% vs 55% MVIC); gluteus medius did not differ across variations.
findings.locator: Table 1 and Table 2 (Collazo Garcia et al. 2018 rows); Results
findings.population: 7 experienced male personal trainers, 40% 1RM, 8 reps

exercises.name: hip thrust with intended hip external rotation (rotation hip thrust)

findings.finding: Placing the feet farther from the hips in the hip thrust raised hamstring EMG (semitendinosus and biceps femoris about 70-72% vs 32-41% MVIC) and lowered rectus femoris and vasti EMG (3-11% vs 6-35%) versus the standard foot position; 7 men.
findings.locator: Table 2 (Collazo Garcia et al. 2018 rows); Results text after Table 2
findings.population: 7 experienced male personal trainers, 40% 1RM

findings.finding: Two potentiation trials (handball and soccer players, n=18 each) found faster 5-20 m sprint times after barbell hip thrust sets at 50-85% RM or optimal-power loads; two further acute studies reported only associations with acceleration or horizontal force.
findings.locator: Results, Motor performance; Table 3 (Dello Iacono et al. 2018; Dello Iacono and Seitz 2018; Loturco et al. 2018; Williams et al. 2018)
findings.population: Four acute studies of trained athletes (n=12-18 each)

exercises.name: barbell hip thrust potentiation sets (50% RM, 85% RM, optimal-power load)

findings.finding: Across four 6-8 week training studies, two reported hip thrust training improved sprint times (one versus front squat over 10-20 m; one 40-yard sprint) and two found no improvement versus control (40 m sprint; 30 m sprint and horizontal jump).
findings.locator: Results, Motor performance; Table 3 (Contreras 2017; Zweifel 2017; Bishop 2017; Lin 2017); Discussion
findings.population: Four chronic studies, 6-8 wk, athletes or trained adults (n=20-26 each)

findings.finding: Over 6 weeks, hip thrust training cut 10-m and 20-m sprint times by 1.05% and 1.67% versus +0.10% and -0.66% with front squats; between-group effects possibly favoured hip thrust (d=0.32 and 0.39, 90% confidence limits crossing zero).
findings.population: 24 adolescent male rugby and rowing athletes aged 14-17 (13 hip thrust, 11 front squat), 6 wk, 2 sessions/wk

findings.finding: Vertical jump height rose 7.30% after front squat training versus 3.42% after hip thrust training; the between-group effect possibly favoured the front squat (d=-0.47, 90% CL -1.20 to 0.23).
findings.population: 24 adolescent male rugby and rowing athletes aged 14-17, 6 wk

findings.finding: Horizontal jump distance improved similarly (hip thrust +2.38%, front squat +1.71%); neither programme was clearly better (d=0.15, 90% CL -0.57 to 0.87).
findings.population: 24 adolescent male rugby and rowing athletes aged 14-17, 6 wk

findings.finding: Front squat 3RM rose 12.85% with front squat training versus 7.10% with hip thrust training; the between-group effect possibly favoured the front squat (d=-0.55, 90% CL -1.25 to 0.15).
findings.locator: Results, Within-Group and Between-Group Comparisons; Table 3
findings.population: 24 adolescent male rugby and rowing athletes aged 14-17, 6 wk

findings.finding: Hip thrust training raised hip thrust 3RM 42.76% versus 21.06% and isometric mid-thigh pull peak force 10.22% versus 1.90% with front squats; both very likely favoured the hip thrust (d=1.35, 90% CL 0.65-2.05; r=0.46, 0.14-0.69).
findings.population: 24 adolescent male rugby and rowing athletes aged 14-17, 6 wk

findings.finding: 45-degree hip extension grew biceps femoris long head volume 6.72% more than Nordic curls (95% CI 0.32-13.11, d=1.03, p=0.037); Nordic vs control was non-significant (5.39%, p=0.122). Both lengthened its fascicles similarly (Nordic +2.22 cm, hip extension +1.33 cm; between-group p>0.05).
findings.locator: Results, Hamstring muscle volumes and BFLH fascicle length; Figures 4-5 (accepted manuscript)
findings.population: 30 recreationally active men (10 per group), 10 wk, 20 sessions

findings.finding: Semitendinosus volume rose more than control after both Nordic (21.21% difference, d=2.50) and hip extension training (14.32%, d=2.16); Nordic and hip extension did not differ (6.90%, 95% CI -2.77 to 16.56, p=0.239).
findings.locator: Results, Hamstring muscle volumes (between-group comparisons); Figure 5
findings.population: 30 recreationally active men (10 per group), 10 wk

findings.finding: Only hip extension grew semimembranosus beyond control (8.95%, p=0.007; Nordic 3.38%, p=0.636). Both grew biceps femoris short head beyond control (Nordic 15.29%, hip extension 8.51%). Nordic growth concentrated in semitendinosus and short head; hip extension was more even.
findings.locator: Results, Hamstring muscle volumes (between- and within-group); Discussion paragraph 4
findings.population: 30 recreationally active men (10 per group), 10 wk

findings.finding: Both exercises raised strength similarly: Nordic eccentric knee-flexor force +97.38 N (Nordic) vs +110.47 N (hip extension), post-training gap 29.16 N (p=0.999); 45-degree hip extension 3RM +26.00 kg vs +41.00 kg, gap 11.50 kg (p=0.082). Controls did not change.
findings.locator: Results, Strength (Nordic eccentric strength test; hip extension strength test); Figures 7-8
findings.population: 30 recreationally active men (10 per group), 10 wk

findings.finding: Adductor longus peak EMG varied widely across eight hip adduction exercises (14% to 108% of MVC, p<0.0001); the authors single out the Copenhagen Adduction and elastic-band hip adduction as dynamic high-intensity options. Per-exercise values are not in the abstract.
findings.population: 40 healthy elite male soccer players, single session

exercises.name: six other hip adduction exercises (not named in abstract)

findings.finding: Across the same adduction exercises, gluteus medius, rectus abdominis and external oblique peak EMG stayed relatively low (5% to 48% of MVC).
findings.population: 40 healthy elite male soccer players, single session

findings.finding: Adding an 8-week progressive Copenhagen Adduction programme to usual in-season training raised eccentric hip adduction strength 35.7% (p<0.001), with no within-group change in controls (p>0.335) and a significant group-by-time interaction (p<0.025).
findings.population: 24 U-19 sub-elite male football players from 2 teams, 8 wk in-season

exercises.name: Copenhagen Adduction programme plus usual training

findings.finding: The same Copenhagen Adduction programme also raised eccentric hip abduction strength 20.3% (p=0.003) and the adduction-to-abduction strength ratio 12.3% (p=0.019), while controls showed no within-group change.
findings.population: 24 U-19 sub-elite male football players from 2 teams, 8 wk in-season

exercises.name: Copenhagen Adduction programme plus usual training

findings.finding: Gluteus medius EMG was highest in side-lying hip abduction (81 +/- 42% MVIC), significantly above both clam variants (40% and 38%), lunges (48%) and hops (48%).
findings.population: 21 healthy, physically active adults, single session

findings.finding: Gluteus maximus EMG reached 59% MVIC in both the single-limb squat and single-limb deadlift, significantly more than lateral band walk (27%), clam (34%), and forward and transverse hops (35% each).
findings.population: 21 healthy, physically active adults, single session

findings.finding: Single-limb squat and single-limb deadlift activated the gluteals similarly: gluteus medius 64% vs 59% MVIC and gluteus maximus 59% vs 59% MVIC.
findings.population: 21 healthy, physically active adults, single session

findings.finding: Highest gluteus maximus %MVIC came from cross-over step-up (103%, 1 study), rotational single-leg squat (79%, 1 study) and lateral step-up (up to 113.8% with a 45.7 cm box; 49.6% averaged over 6 studies). Monster walks gave only 4-6%.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, Table 1; 'Very High' and 'Low EMG Activity Exercise' sections
findings.population: 23 EMG studies, 467 injury-free participants of any age/sex

findings.finding: Gluteus medius peaked in side bridge with abduction (103% MVIC dominant leg down, 88.8% up; n=26), near-maximal banded standing abduction (Borg CR10 >=7; 101%; n=16) and side-lying abduction (up to 81.2%; 45.2% across 9 studies); four clamshell variants gave the lowest values (12-18%).
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, Tables 1 and 2; 'Very High' and 'Low EMG Activity Exercise' sections
findings.population: 23 EMG studies, 467 injury-free participants of any age/sex

exercises.name: standing hip abduction with band at ankle

findings.finding: Averaged by position, standing exercises gave 34.7% (gluteus maximus) and 47.2% (gluteus medius) MVIC versus 30.4% and 41.9% side-lying. The seated abduction machine averaged about 67-69% and 65%, but only one study (n=16) tested it.
findings.locator: Results, Table 4 and 'Summary of positions'; Conclusion
findings.population: 23 EMG studies, 467 injury-free participants; seated data from 1 study (n=16)

findings.finding: Raising effort from Borg CR10 <=2 to >=7 lifted gluteus medius activity from 73% to 101% MVIC in banded standing abduction and from 53% to 80% on the seated machine; gluteus maximus rose less (59% to 73%; 67% to 70%).
findings.locator: Results, Tables 1 and 3; Appendix 1 (Brandt et al.)
findings.population: 16 women (mean age 45.7 y) in one included study (Brandt et al.)

exercises.name: standing hip abduction with band at ankle, Borg <=2
standing hip abduction with band at ankle, Borg >=7

findings.finding: Placing the band lower on the leg raised activity: lateral stepping gave 35% gluteus medius MVIC with the band at the foot, 29% at the ankle and 24% at the knee; monster walks gave 27%, 25% and 19%. Gluteus maximus stayed at 4-8%.
findings.population: 9 men in one included study (Cambridge et al.)

exercises.name: lateral band walk, band at foot
lateral band walk, band at ankle
lateral band walk, band at knee

findings.finding: Clamshell versions that internally rotate the top leg (knees together, thigh raised, or leg extended) reached 62.4-76.8% gluteus medius MVIC, versus 47.2% for the standard external-rotation clamshell; reviewers suggest them for people who cannot do weight-bearing work.
findings.locator: Table 2 legend; Appendix 1 (Boren et al.); Discussion
findings.population: 26 participants in one included study (Boren et al.)

findings.finding: Free-weight lifts gave the highest rectus abdominis, external oblique and erector spinae activity; stability exercises gave the highest internal oblique and traditional exercises the highest multifidus activity. Most included studies were moderate evidence quality and methods varied.
findings.population: 67 studies, 1247 healthy adults, 233 exercises, 2012-2020

findings.finding: Rectus abdominis peaked in the unstable Bulgarian squat and regular back squat at 6RM (~210% MVIC, one study), then suspended roll-out and front planks (upper 145%, lower 122%); the best floor options were a hands-behind-neck static curl-up (81%) and V-sits (~80%).
findings.population: 67 studies, 1247 healthy adults (rectus abdominis measured in 51 studies)

findings.finding: Internal oblique activity was highest in a front plank with scapular adduction and posterior pelvic tilt (119.92% MVIC), ahead of kettlebell swing with kime (80.8%), Swiss-ball plank with hip extension (76.5%), stir-the-pot (73.5%) and static curl-up (61.7%).
findings.population: 67 studies, 1247 healthy adults (internal oblique measured in 23 studies)

exercises.name: front plank with scapular adduction and posterior pelvic tilt
Swiss-ball front plank with hip extension

findings.finding: External oblique activity was highest in Bulgarian squats (~155% stable, ~148% unstable MVIC) and stir-the-pot (144.2%), then the modified front plank (110.78%) and Swiss-ball plank with hip extension (109.4%); the best curl-up reached 70.74%. Unilateral loaded lifts were recommended.
findings.population: 67 studies, 1247 healthy adults (external oblique measured in 45 studies)

exercises.name: front plank with scapular adduction and posterior pelvic tilt
Swiss-ball front plank with hip extension

findings.finding: Erector spinae activity was greatest in free-weight lifts: barbell deadlift ~90%, hip thrust ~85% and hex-bar deadlift ~80% MVIC, versus ~63% for floor back extension, ~56% on a bench and 61.51% for a suspended bridge.
findings.population: 67 studies, 1247 healthy adults (erector spinae measured in 37 studies)

findings.finding: Lumbar multifidus peaked in prone trunk and leg extensions with active lumbopelvic control (~64% MVIC) and Swiss-ball plank with hip extension (~62%); bent-over row (~58.2%), deadlift (~57.9%) and back squat (~54.8%) were close; bridge and bird dog ~39%.
findings.population: 67 studies, 1247 healthy adults (multifidus measured in only 16 studies)

exercises.name: Swiss-ball front plank with hip extension

findings.finding: Transversus abdominis data were scarce (3 studies): a side-lying sling exercise reached 58.65% MVIC and a hands-behind-neck static curl-up 40.7%; authors still preferred prone and supine sling work for lumbar stabilisation.
findings.population: 3 included studies measured transversus abdominis

findings.finding: Adding a suspension system to the bridge increased trunk-extensor (and abdominal, gluteal, hamstring) recruitment, whereas bridging on a Swiss ball or whole-body wobble board did not raise erector spinae activity.
findings.population: 3 included bridge studies (review refs 45, 50, 82)

findings.finding: Exercises with active trunk extension produced the highest extensor muscle activity and the highest L4-5 compressive loads; leg-extension tasks with the spine held still gave asymmetric, milder trunk-muscle activity and lower spinal load. The abstract gives no numeric values.
findings.population: 13 young men (mean age 21), single session

exercises.name: single-leg extension with spine held isometric
single-leg extension with contralateral arm extension

findings.finding: Adding a contralateral arm extension to single-leg extension increased the exercise's challenge and demand; single-leg extension alone was judged a low-spine-load, mildly challenging starting exercise for extensor strengthening.
findings.population: 13 young men (mean age 21), single session

exercises.name: single-leg extension with contralateral arm extension

findings.finding: During dynamic Roman chair extensions, lumbar extensor EMG was 18% higher with the hips internally rotated than externally rotated (P<=.05).
findings.population: 12 healthy adults (7 men, 5 women, 18-35 y) without low back pain

exercises.name: Roman chair back extension with internal hip rotation
Roman chair back extension with external hip rotation

findings.finding: Changing hip rotation during Roman chair extension did not change gluteal or hamstring EMG (P>.05).
findings.population: 12 healthy adults (7 men, 5 women, 18-35 y) without low back pain

exercises.name: Roman chair back extension with internal hip rotation
Roman chair back extension with external hip rotation

findings.finding: Lumbar extensor EMG was 25% higher when the Roman chair movement used a posture accentuating lumbar lordosis (biphasic) than with a typical posture (P<=.05).
findings.population: 12 healthy adults (7 men, 5 women, 18-35 y) without low back pain

exercises.name: Roman chair back extension with accentuated lumbar lordosis (biphasic)
Roman chair back extension with typical lumbar posture (nonbiphasic)

findings.finding: Gluteal and hamstring EMG did not differ between the accentuated-lordosis and typical lumbar postures during Roman chair extension (P>.05).
findings.population: 12 healthy adults (7 men, 5 women, 18-35 y) without low back pain

exercises.name: Roman chair back extension with accentuated lumbar lordosis (biphasic)
Roman chair back extension with typical lumbar posture (nonbiphasic)

findings.finding: Across deadlift variants, erector spinae and quadriceps generally showed greater activation than gluteus maximus and biceps femoris (9/19 studies). Normalisation methods differed (%MVIC, %peak RMS, raw RMS, %1RM), so values were not pooled.
findings.population: 19 cross-sectional studies, resistance-trained adults (>=6 months), 8-34 per study

exercises.name: conventional deadlift and its variants (muscle-to-muscle comparison)

findings.finding: Reviewers suggested knee-extended hinges (Romanian, stiff-leg deadlift) favour posterior-thigh activity, but their included head-to-head studies showed similar biceps femoris versus the conventional lift (56.66 vs 57.45%; 98.6 vs 100.1% peak RMS); one Romanian deadlift study found erector spinae below both hamstrings.
findings.population: Head-to-head data from 21 trained men (Lee 2018), 14 trained men (Bezerra 2013) and 12 trained men (McAllister 2014)

findings.finding: The hex-bar deadlift produced more vastus lateralis activity than the straight-bar deadlift (concentric 119.9% vs 96.8% of 1RM-normalised EMG).
findings.population: 20 trained men, 65% and 85% 1RM

findings.finding: Versus hex-bar deadlifts, straight-bar deadlifts gave higher concentric biceps femoris (83.5% vs 72.3%) and erector spinae (98.9% vs 88%) 1RM-normalised EMG (n=20); another study found higher biceps femoris (~108% vs ~83% MVIC) but no erector spinae difference (~86% vs ~82%; n=13).
findings.locator: Tables 1, 2 and 5 (Camara et al. 2016; Andersen et al. 2018); Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'
findings.population: 20 trained men (Camara 2016) and 13 trained men at 1RM (Andersen 2018)

findings.finding: At 1RM, the hip thrust produced greater gluteus maximus activation than both the conventional deadlift (~95% MVIC) and the hex-bar deadlift (~88% MVIC).
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 2; Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'
findings.population: 13 trained men, 1RM

findings.finding: Biceps femoris activation was lower in the hip thrust than in the conventional deadlift (deadlift ~108% MVIC; hex-bar ~83%).
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 2; Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'
findings.population: 13 trained men, 1RM

findings.finding: Erector spinae activation did not differ between the hip thrust, conventional deadlift (~86% MVIC) and hex-bar deadlift (~82% MVIC).
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 2; Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'
findings.population: 13 trained men, 1RM

findings.finding: The sumo deadlift produced more vastus lateralis (48% vs 40% MVIC) and vastus medialis (44% vs 36%) activity than the conventional deadlift; gluteus maximus (37% vs 35%) and hamstring values were close.
findings.population: 13 men, 12RM load

findings.finding: The conventional deadlift produced more medial gastrocnemius activity than the sumo deadlift (no values given in the review).
findings.population: 13 men, 12RM load

findings.finding: The conventional deadlift gave higher gluteus maximus (51.52% vs 46.88% peak RMS) and rectus femoris (58.57% vs 25.26%) activity than the Romanian deadlift; biceps femoris was similar (57.45% vs 56.66%).
findings.population: 21 trained men, 70% of Romanian deadlift 1RM

findings.finding: The conventional deadlift produced more vastus lateralis activity than the stiff-leg deadlift (128.3% vs 101.1% peak RMS), while biceps femoris (100.1% vs 98.6%) and lumbar multifidus (112.7% vs 106%) were similar.
findings.population: 14 trained men, 70% 1RM

findings.finding: The stiff-leg deadlift produced more medial gastrocnemius activity than the conventional deadlift (no values given in the review).
findings.population: 14 trained men, 70% 1RM

findings.finding: Front and back squats produced greater gluteus maximus activity than the deadlift (94% and 80% vs 72% of 1RM-normalised EMG); front and back squat did not differ significantly.
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 5 (Korak et al. 2018); Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'
findings.population: 13 trained women, 75% 1RM

findings.finding: A modified single-leg squat produced significantly greater gluteus maximus and hamstring activity than the back squat and stiff-leg deadlift (stiff-leg deadlift concentric: 51.1% and 39.8% MVIC).
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 2 (McCurdy et al. 2018); Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'
findings.population: 18 trained women, 8RM loads

findings.finding: Nordic hamstring exercise and 45-degree hip extension (Bourne), and Nordic plus seated leg curl (Ebben), gave more hamstring activity than bilateral or unilateral stiff-leg deadlifts (Ebben: 49% and 48% MVIC). The review's summary table describes Bourne's result partly differently.
findings.locator: Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'; Tables 1 and 2 (Bourne 2017; Ebben 2009)
findings.population: Trained men (Bourne 2017) and 34 adults at 6RM (Ebben 2009)

findings.finding: Leg curl versus hip-hinge evidence conflicts: the review reports Schoenfeld (n=10) both as favouring the prone leg curl for biceps femoris and as favouring the stiff-leg deadlift for upper hamstrings, while McAllister (n=12) found more biceps femoris in the Romanian deadlift.
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 2; Discussion 'Comparing Deadlift to other exercises'
findings.population: 10 trained men (Schoenfeld 2015) and 12 trained men (McAllister 2014)

findings.finding: Unilateral and bilateral stiff-leg deadlifts produced similar hamstring activity (48% vs 49% MVIC; similar biceps femoris and semitendinosus in a second study), though semitendinosus was relatively higher in the single-leg version (~62% vs ~50% concentric).
findings.population: 34 adults at 6RM (Ebben 2009); trained men at 12RM (Bourne 2017)

findings.finding: Free-weight stiff-leg deadlift gave higher peak concentric activity than an elastic-band version for gluteus maximus (~42% vs ~27% MVIC), biceps femoris (~38% vs ~20%) and semitendinosus (~44% vs ~23%).
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 2 (Iversen et al. 2017); 'Other Deadlift variations'
findings.population: 29 adults (17 men, 12 women), 10RM

findings.finding: The barbell deadlift produced more gluteus maximus (~47% vs ~30% peak RMS) and erector spinae (~73% vs ~53-58%) activity than a walk-in machine deadlift, which instead produced more vastus lateralis activity (~63-80% vs ~48%).
findings.population: 15 adults (13 men, 2 women), 80% 3RM

findings.finding: A standard stable-ground deadlift produced greater overall lumbar and thoracic multifidus and erector spinae activity than deadlifts performed on a BOSU or T-Bow unstable device.
findings.population: 31 trained adults

findings.finding: The deadlift produced greater upper lumbar erector spinae activity than the parallel squat.
findings.population: 16 adults (8 men, 8 women), 80% 1RM

findings.finding: A standard deadlift produced greater gluteus maximus activity than a deadlift with chains (82.5% vs 76.8% of 1RM-normalised EMG).
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 5 (Nijem et al. 2016); 'Other Deadlift variations'
findings.population: 13 men, 85% 1RM

findings.finding: Erector spinae read 341 raw RMS units with free weight alone, 330 with two ceiling-anchored elastic bands and 357 with four; the review summarises this as more bands raising erector spinae activity, without stating which contrasts were significant.
findings.locator: Table 1, Table 4 (Andersen et al. 2019); 'Other Deadlift variations'
findings.population: 15 trained men, 2RM

exercises.name: free-weight deadlift plus two ceiling-anchored elastic bands
free-weight deadlift plus four ceiling-anchored elastic bands

findings.finding: The good morning showed a muscle pattern similar to the Romanian deadlift, with more semitendinosus and less biceps femoris activity; reviewers present it as a substitute when loading the back rather than lifting from the floor.
findings.population: 12 trained men, 85% 1RM

findings.finding: A deadlift with a thick-grip attachment increased forearm muscle activity but significantly lowered 1RM compared with the standard bar.
findings.population: 15 men, 1RM

findings.finding: Versus the bodyweight squat, bodyweight deadlift, superman and side bridge, the 80% 1RM squat produced 56, 56.6, 65.5 and 53.1% more lumbosacral erector spinae EMG, and the 80% 1RM deadlift 66.7, 65.5, 69.3 and 68.6% more upper lumbar erector spinae EMG.
findings.population: 16 subjects. The abstract gives no sex breakdown, but MeSH tags both Male and Female.

findings.finding: At 80% 1RM, which lift won depended on the region. The squat produced 34.5% more lumbosacral erector spinae EMG than the deadlift. The deadlift produced 12.9% more upper lumbar erector spinae EMG than the squat.
findings.population: 16 subjects. The abstract gives no sex breakdown, but MeSH tags both Male and Female.

findings.finding: Lower abdominal and external oblique EMG showed no significant differences across the heavy and bodyweight squats and deadlifts, the superman and the side bridge.
findings.population: 16 subjects. The abstract gives no sex breakdown, but MeSH tags both Male and Female.

findings.finding: Only the isolated lumbar extension group significantly increased isometric lumbar extension torque, at 6 of 7 joint angles. Romanian deadlift training did not significantly increase lumbar extension torque, and controls did not change.
findings.population: 36 trained men (mean age 24.9 y), 10 weeks; group sizes not given in abstract

findings.finding: Romanian deadlift 1RM rose in the deadlift group (143.3±23.4 to 166.3±21.9 kg) and in the isolated lumbar extension group (135.8±23.1 to 146.0±25.5 kg). Controls did not change. The abstract gives no between-group test.
findings.population: 36 trained men (mean age 24.9 y), 10 weeks; group sizes not given in abstract

findings.finding: Over 6 months, MRI cross-sectional area of the rectus abdominis, obliques, psoas major, quadratus lumborum and erector spinae grew in both groups: 4.4-13.4% with stabilization plus soccer and 5.5-10.9% with soccer only. Group had no significant effect.
findings.population: 28 male youth soccer players aged 12-13 (16 training, 12 control), 6 months

exercises.name: stabilization program (elbow-toe, elbow-heel, side bridge, modified one-legged squat, bent-knee push-up) plus soccer training

findings.finding: Isokinetic hip extension peak torque at 1.05 rad/s rose more with stabilization exercise plus soccer (40.8%) than with soccer alone (17.4%). The abstract gives no result for hip flexion torque.
findings.population: 28 male youth soccer players aged 12-13 (16 training, 12 control), 6 months

exercises.name: stabilization program (elbow-toe, elbow-heel, side bridge, modified one-legged squat, bent-knee push-up) plus soccer training

findings.finding: Only the stabilization-plus-soccer group significantly improved squat jump (5.0%) and countermovement jump (6.8%); these are within-group results. 15-m sprint time improved similarly in both groups (-1.4% vs -1.6%), with no group effect.
findings.population: 28 male youth soccer players aged 12-13 (16 training, 12 control), 6 months

exercises.name: stabilization program (elbow-toe, elbow-heel, side bridge, modified one-legged squat, bent-knee push-up) plus soccer training

findings.finding: Trunk extensor strength rose 5% over time (d=0.86) with core training on either surface, and surface made no difference (no group-by-time interaction). There was no non-core control arm, so the gain cannot be attributed to core work alone.
findings.population: 39 elite male youth soccer players aged 17±1, 9 weeks

exercises.name: core strength training on unstable surfaces (e.g., stability trainer pad, Swiss ball)
core strength training on stable surfaces (floor, bench)

findings.finding: In both groups, 10-20-m sprint time improved 3% (d=2.56) and kicking performance 1% (d=1.28), with no group-by-time interaction. Countermovement jump is not among the outcomes the abstract reports as improved.
findings.population: 39 elite male youth soccer players aged 17±1, 9 weeks

exercises.name: core strength training on unstable surfaces (e.g., stability trainer pad, Swiss ball)
core strength training on stable surfaces (floor, bench)

findings.finding: Agility time was measured but showed no group-by-time interaction between unstable- and stable-surface core training. It is also not among the outcomes the abstract reports as improving over time.
findings.population: 39 elite male youth soccer players aged 17±1, 9 weeks

exercises.name: core strength training on unstable surfaces (e.g., stability trainer pad, Swiss ball)
core strength training on stable surfaces (floor, bench)

findings.finding: Versus usual-training controls, core training improved vertical jump (SMD 0.69, 95% CI 0.32-1.06; 333 participants; I²=62%; GRADE moderate). The GRADE table lists 11 studies, whereas the Results text says 8 studies were analysed.
findings.locator: Table 3 (GRADE summary of findings); Results, jumping performance section; Figure 5 (upper)
findings.population: Healthy athletes and students older than 12 (youth and adults, mixed sports), core programs of 4-12 weeks. Jump studies included 483 participants in total; 333 were in the vertical jump pooled analysis.

findings.finding: Versus usual-training controls, core training improved horizontal jump (SMD 0.84, 95% CI 0.16-1.52; 5 studies, 332 participants; I²=85%). The authors rated this evidence low certainty because of very serious inconsistency.
findings.locator: Table 3 (GRADE summary of findings); Results, jumping performance section; Figure 5 (upper)
findings.population: Healthy athletes and students older than 12 (youth and adults, mixed sports), core programs of 4-12 weeks; 332 participants in the horizontal jump pooled analysis

findings.finding: Core training did not significantly improve throwing/hitting velocity (SMD 0.30, -0.10 to 0.71; 7 trials, 220 participants). It did improve throwing/hitting distance (SMD 3.42, 0.35-6.49; 2-3 trials; I²=97%). GRADE rated both low.
findings.locator: Table 3 (GRADE summary of findings); Results, throwing/hitting section; Figure 4
findings.population: Healthy athletes older than 12 in throwing/hitting sports (tennis, handball, baseball, golf), 280 participants, core programs of 4-12 weeks

findings.finding: Both approaches beat control. Isolated core training scored jump SMD 1.01 and throw/hit 0.52; combined core training scored jump 0.86 and throw/hit 1.67. The authors found no significant difference between the two.
findings.locator: Results, jumping and throwing/hitting subgroup analyses (Figures 4-5, lower panels); Conclusions
findings.population: Healthy athletes and students older than 12, core programs of 4-12 weeks (subgroup analysis)

exercises.name: core training combined with plyometric, upper-limb or lower-limb training

findings.finding: After 12 months, maximal isometric neck strength (flexion/extension/rotation) rose 110/69/76% with elastic-band training at 80% of maximum. It rose 28/16/29% with light head-lift endurance training and 10/7/10% in controls (P<.001). Neck muscular endurance was not measured.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results (maximal isometric neck strength, Figure 2)
findings.population: 180 female office workers aged 25-53 with chronic nonspecific neck pain, 12 months (clinical population)

exercises.name: high-intensity isometric elastic-band neck strength training (about 80% of maximum)
light dynamic neck endurance training (head lifts)

findings.finding: Plyometric training beat control groups on all four jump tests: squat jump +4.7% (ES 0.44), countermovement jump +8.7% (ES 0.88), countermovement jump with arm swing +7.5% (ES 0.74), drop jump +4.7% (ES 0.62). Publication bias flagged for CMJ and CMJA.
findings.population: 1024 healthy subjects (83% male), aged 11-29 y, athletes and non-athletes, programmes of 4-24 weeks

exercises.name: plyometric jump training (drop jumps, countermovement jumps, mixed body-weight jumps)

findings.finding: Subgroup analysis found no significant difference in jump-height gains between drop-jump-only, countermovement-jump-only and mixed-jump programmes on any of the four jump tests; athletes and non-athletes gained similarly. The author notes jumping technique was poorly controlled.
findings.population: 1024 healthy subjects (83% male), aged 11-29 y, 4-24 week programmes
