findings.finding: Meta-regression: more total plyometric sessions (range 12-60) predicted larger gains in squat jump (p=0.002) and arm-swing countermovement jump (p=0.004); programme weeks, total foot contacts (468-7500), age and sex showed no significant relationship.
findings.population: 1024 healthy subjects, 12-60 total sessions over 4-24 weeks

exercises.name: plyometric programmes with more total sessions
plyometric programmes with fewer total sessions

findings.finding: Across 107 plyometric-group effect sizes, mean vertical jump gain was ES 0.84 (3.90 cm) versus ES 0.13 (0.84 cm) across 44 control-group effect sizes (p<0.05). Effect sizes were within-group pre-post changes, not control-adjusted differences.
findings.locator: Results (first paragraph); Discussion. Full text read from the typeset ahead-of-print PDF (pages 1-12) hosted at paulogentil.com; publisher page paywalled
findings.population: Healthy athletes and non-athletes in 56 controlled studies, mostly men, programmes of about 3-36 weeks

findings.finding: Programmes mixing squat jumps, countermovement jumps and drop jumps gave ES 1.46 (11 ES), significantly above single forms: drop jumps 0.66 (45), squat jumps 0.54 (9), countermovement jumps 0.40 (7); CMJ+DJ 0.66, SJ+DJ 0.47, other mixes 0.56.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Type of plyometric exercises); Results; Discussion
findings.population: Healthy athletes and non-athletes in 56 controlled studies, mostly men

exercises.name: squat jump + countermovement jump + drop jump combined

findings.finding: Adding external weight to jumps did not significantly change vertical jump gains: added weight ES 0.84 (16 ES), body weight only 0.67 (86), hydraulic machines 0.38 (2); p=0.45.
findings.population: Healthy athletes and non-athletes in 56 controlled studies, mostly men

findings.finding: Combining plyometrics with other training did not significantly alter jump gains (p=0.93): plyometrics alone ES 0.68 (78 ES), plus resistance training 0.76 (17), plus electrostimulation 0.94 (3), plus aerobic 0.75 (4), plus flexibility 0.69 (4), water-based 0.33 (3).
findings.locator: Table 3 (Combination with other types of exercise); Discussion
findings.population: Healthy athletes and non-athletes in 56 controlled studies, mostly men

findings.finding: High-intensity plyometric sessions produced larger vertical jump gains (ES 1.22, 21 ES) than moderate-intensity (0.57, 47 ES) or low-intensity sessions (0.56, 36 ES); p<0.001.
findings.population: Healthy athletes and non-athletes in 56 controlled studies, mostly men

findings.finding: Jump gains correlated with programme weeks (r=0.45), total sessions (r=0.52) and jumps per session (r=0.39), each reported at p=0.01; weekly frequency, drop height, session length and rest between sets did not. Abstract proposes >10 weeks, >20 sessions, >50 jumps/session.
findings.population: Healthy athletes and non-athletes in 56 controlled studies, mostly men

exercises.name: longer plyometric programmes with more sessions and jumps per session

findings.finding: Plyometric groups improved sprint times by mean ES 0.37 (-0.081 s; 41 ES) versus ES 0.03 (-0.013 s; 15 ES) in controls (p<0.05); the effect did not differ significantly across sprint distances from 10 m to 100 m.
findings.locator: Results; Table 5; Discussion. Full text read from the published typeset PDF (pp. 575-584) hosted at paulogentil.com; publisher page paywalled
findings.population: 26 studies of healthy athletes, PE students and untrained adults (including women aged about 40-65 y), mostly male, aged about 11-65 y, 4-12 week programmes

findings.finding: Type of plyometrics affected sprint gains (ANOVA p=0.009): mixed programmes ES 0.41 (28 ES) and one squat jump + drop jump group 0.76 were marked significant; drop-jump-only 0.27 (11 ES), squat-jump-only -0.16 (1 ES). Horizontal-jump advice is discussion, not a tested moderator.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Type of plyometric exercises); Results; Discussion
findings.population: 26 studies of healthy athletes and students, mostly male

findings.finding: Weighted plyometric jumps gave no significant sprint benefit over body-weight jumps: ES 0.46 (3 ES) versus 0.35 (38 ES); p=0.61.
findings.population: 26 studies of healthy athletes and students, mostly male

findings.finding: For sprint improvement, plyometrics combined with weight training (ES 0.28, 11 ES) or electrostimulation (0.26, 1 ES) did not differ significantly from plyometrics alone (0.40, 28 ES); p=0.61. Workloads were not equated between groups.
findings.locator: Table 3 (Combination with other types of exercise); Discussion
findings.population: 26 studies of healthy athletes and students, mostly male

findings.finding: Sprint gains correlated positively with sessions per week (r=0.36) and jumps per session (r=0.37), negatively with programme weeks (r=-0.51) and rest between sets (r=-0.66). Session intensity was not significant (p=0.058). Text and table disagree on jumps-per-session significance.
findings.locator: Table 4; Table 3 (Intensity of session); Results; Discussion
findings.population: 26 studies of healthy athletes and students, mostly male, 4-12 week programmes

exercises.name: shorter plyometric programmes with more weekly sessions, more jumps and shorter rests

findings.finding: Plyometric programmes combining drop jumps, vertical jumps and standing long jumps improved change-of-direction ability more than programmes using one jump form. The abstract reports no effect sizes for this comparison.
findings.population: 24 plyometric training studies of male and female athletes, including basketball players

exercises.name: combined drop jump + vertical jump + standing long jump programme

findings.finding: Plyometric training improved change-of-direction ability. Programmes of about 7 weeks, 2 sessions/week, moderate intensity, roughly 100 jumps per session and 72 h rest tended to improve it. Fitter participants and basketball players gained more; men and women responded similarly.
findings.population: 24 plyometric training studies of male and female athletes

findings.finding: No training form was superior for change of direction. Mean gain, trained vs control: plyometrics 5.26% vs 0.98% (49 groups), strength 3.32% vs -0.40% (26), combined 3.18% vs 0.8% (23), PAP 2.58% vs -0.26% (8), COD drills 2.4% vs 1.2% (20), sprint 2% vs 0.12% (6).
findings.locator: Results - Plyometric Training, Training for PAP and Strength Training, Specific COD and Sprint Training, Combined Training; Figs 4-7; Practical Consequences and Applications
findings.population: 1652 court- and field-sport athletes (1146 soccer players; 110 of 132 groups male), mean age 16.5 y, mostly 4-10 week interventions

findings.finding: Authors' synthesis: strength training suits strength-oriented COD (turns of 90 degrees or more), plyometrics helps both strength- and velocity-oriented COD, sprint training suits velocity-oriented COD. COD drills transfer mainly to matching tasks. Plyometric effect sizes showed no consistent trend by COD type.
findings.locator: Conclusion; Practical Consequences and Applications; Discussion - Plyometric Training and Specific COD Training
findings.population: 1652 court- and field-sport athletes, mostly young male soccer players

findings.finding: Every plyometric group used drop and/or countermovement jumps. The largest improvement (14.88%) came from drop plus countermovement jump training, and the authors judged that combination better than single-exercise plyometrics. In one study, drop jumps from an individually optimal height beat a fixed height.
findings.locator: Results - Plyometric Training; Discussion - Plyometric Training; Table 1
findings.population: 49 plyometric groups of young (about 25 y or younger) court- and field-sport athletes, mostly 2 sessions/week

findings.finding: About half the strength groups exceeded ES 0.8 for change of direction. Two of the three largest effects (ES above 2) came from half squats at 70-90% 1RM, trained twice weekly for 8 weeks. Nordic hamstring training improved COD by 2.46%. Authors advise pairing squats with horizontal-force exercises.
findings.locator: Discussion - Strength Training; Results - Training for PAP and Strength Training; Table 2
findings.population: Strength-training groups of adolescent and young adult court- and field-sport athletes, mostly 2 sessions/week for 6-8 weeks

findings.finding: Olympic weightlifting training (at least 6 weeks) increased vertical jump height 7.7% more than control (ES 0.62, p=0.03; 3 studies), in resistance-trained athletes and physical education students.
findings.population: 232 resistance-trained participants (175 athletes, 57 PE students), mean age 19.5 y, interventions of at least 6 weeks

findings.finding: Olympic weightlifting training increased vertical jump height 5.1% more than traditional resistance training (ES 0.64, p=0.00004; 4 studies).
findings.population: 232 resistance-trained participants (175 athletes, 57 PE students), mean age 19.5 y

findings.finding: Vertical jump gains did not differ between Olympic weightlifting and plyometric training (3 studies). The authors conclude either method can be used to improve jump height.
findings.population: 232 resistance-trained participants (175 athletes, 57 PE students), mean age 19.5 y

findings.finding: Versus traditional resistance training, weightlifting training improved countermovement jump more (9 studies, g=0.95, 95% CI 0.04–1.87). Squat jump (5 studies, g=0.36, CI −0.38 to 1.09) and linear sprint (4 studies, g=1.04, CI −0.03 to 2.39) gains did not differ significantly; heterogeneity high.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Traditional Resistance Training' subsection (forest plots)
findings.population: 10 studies with a TRT arm (TRT n=127); across all 16 studies median age 20.3 y, mostly male, little weightlifting or resistance-training experience; median 8 weeks

findings.finding: Weightlifting training increased the load lifted in weightlifting movements more than traditional resistance training (4 studies, g=1.35, 95% CI 0.20–2.51, p=0.02); the authors attribute this to training specificity. Heterogeneity was high.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Traditional Resistance Training'; Discussion
findings.population: 4 studies with a TRT arm reporting weightlifting load; mostly young males with limited weightlifting experience; median 8 weeks

findings.finding: General strength gains did not differ between weightlifting and traditional resistance training (8 studies, g=0.19, 95% CI −0.31 to 0.69, p=0.46). All programmes in this comparison included squats; removing fair-quality studies gave a small non-significant edge to traditional training.
findings.locator: Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Traditional Resistance Training' and 'Risk of Bias' (sensitivity analysis, ESM Appendix 5); Discussion
findings.population: Studies with a TRT arm; mostly young males with limited resistance-training experience; median 8 weeks

findings.finding: Change-of-direction speed gains did not differ significantly between weightlifting and traditional resistance training (2 studies, g=1.21, 95% CI −1.41 to 3.83, p=0.36); the estimate is very imprecise.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Traditional Resistance Training'
findings.population: 2 studies with a TRT arm and a CODS test; young athletes

findings.finding: Weightlifting and plyometric training produced similar power gains: countermovement jump (6 studies, g=0.31, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.67), squat jump (5 studies, g=0.34, CI −0.04 to 0.73) and 20–30 m sprint (4 studies, g=0.20, CI −0.23 to 0.63), all non-significant.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Plyometric Training'; Discussion (sprint distances 20–30 m)
findings.population: 6 studies with a PLYO arm (PLYO n=61); young, mostly male, under 2 years of training experience

findings.finding: Strength gains did not differ significantly between weightlifting and plyometric training (4 studies, g=0.69, 95% CI −0.37 to 1.75, p=0.20), with high heterogeneity (I²=77%).
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Plyometric Training'
findings.population: 4 studies with a PLYO arm; young, under 2 years of training experience

findings.finding: Change-of-direction speed gains were similar after weightlifting and plyometric training (3 studies, g=0.17, 95% CI −0.35 to 0.68, p=0.52).
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Plyometric Training'
findings.population: 3 studies with a PLYO arm; young athletes

findings.finding: Compared with no added training, weightlifting training improved countermovement jump (5 studies, g=0.66, 95% CI 0.19–1.13), squat jump (3 studies, g=1.34, CI 0.74–1.95) and sprint speed (3 studies, g=0.66, CI 0.05–1.27).
findings.population: 5 studies with a control arm (control n=53); young athletes, typically 3 sessions/week for about 8 weeks

findings.finding: Compared with no added training, weightlifting training produced a large strength gain (2 studies, g=2.40, 95% CI 1.50–3.30, p<0.001).
findings.population: 2 studies with a control arm; young athletes

findings.finding: Compared with no added training, weightlifting training gave a moderate but non-significant change-of-direction improvement (3 studies, g=0.67, 95% CI −0.27 to 1.62, p=0.16; I²=73%).
findings.locator: Results, 'Weightlifting Training Versus Control Group'; Discussion
findings.population: 3 studies with a control arm; young athletes

findings.finding: Weightlifting exercises improved countermovement jump more than traditional resistance training (4 studies, n=78; ES 0.72±0.23, 95% CI 0.26–1.19, p=0.002); mean jump gains were 7.5% versus 2.1%.
findings.population: 4 trials comparing weightlifting with traditional resistance training (total n=78)

findings.finding: Weightlifting exercises and plyometric training improved countermovement jump similarly (4 studies, n=76; ES 0.15±0.23, 95% CI −0.30 to 0.60, p=0.518); mean gains were 8.8% versus 8.1%.
findings.population: 4 trials comparing weightlifting with plyometric training (total n=76)

findings.finding: Across 15 studies (510 subjects), gains in free-weight back-squat strength correlated strongly with sprint improvement (r=−0.77, p=0.0001); resistance training improved sprint performance overall (ES −0.87, mean 3.11% faster). This is pre-post and correlational, not a head-to-head comparison.
findings.population: 510 subjects in 15 resistance-training studies (26 experimental, 11 control groups); athlete status not verified beyond the abstract

findings.finding: Sprint transfer was not significantly moderated by resistance-training method (p=0.06), average load (%1RM, p=0.34), programme duration, exercises per session, sets or reps. It was associated with training level (p=0.03), body mass (r=0.35), weekly frequency (r=0.50) and inter-set rest (r=−0.47).
findings.population: 510 subjects across 15 studies; direction of the frequency and rest correlations cannot be interpreted without the full text

findings.finding: Across 48 studies (1,485 subjects), specific sprint training (free, resisted, assisted) gave moderate gains (ES −1.00, −3.23%). Non-specific resistance/plyometric training peaked at 31+ m (ES −0.43, −1.65%); combined training peaked at 0–10 m (ES −0.59, −2.81%).
findings.population: 1,485 subjects from a range of athletic backgrounds; sprint distances 0–10 m to 31+ m

findings.finding: Heavy back squats (75–90% 1RM) and maximal-effort jump squats (0–30% 1RM) improved jump peak power (17.7%±9.3% vs 17.6%±4.5%) and 40 m sprint (2.2%±1.9% vs 3.6%±2.3%) with no significant between-group differences.
findings.population: 24 relatively weak men with proficient squat technique; 3 sessions/week for 10 weeks

findings.finding: Heavy back-squat training raised squat 1RM significantly more than jump-squat training (31.2%±11.3% vs 4.5%±7.1%). Citing similar short-term jump and sprint gains plus the potential long-term value of greater maximal strength, the authors favour strength training for relatively weak men.
findings.population: 24 relatively weak men; 3 sessions/week for 10 weeks

findings.finding: The review cites a 14-study meta-analysis in which >60% 1RM training beat ≤60% 1RM for dynamic 1RM strength (ES 0.58), in upper and lower body alike. On isometric tests the advantage was small and non-significant (ES 0.16). Light loads still raise strength.
findings.population: Studies pooled in the cited 14-study meta-analysis (population not detailed in the review); applies to resistance exercise generally, not specific muscles

findings.finding: Several cited trials found larger 1RM gains with 1–5 reps than with 8–12 reps, though not all did. The review suggests this dose-response is more pronounced in resistance-trained lifters. No pooled estimate is given.
findings.population: Cited trials (participant details not given in this paragraph of the review)

findings.finding: In a cited meta-analysis, whole-muscle hypertrophy did not differ between >60% and <60% 1RM loads (ES difference 0.03, 95% CI −0.16 to 0.22), in upper and lower body. The review concludes growth is similar across loads ≥~30% 1RM when sets approach failure.
findings.population: Cited studies in untrained, trained and older adults; applies to resistance exercise generally

findings.finding: In a cited 12-week within-subject trial (elbow flexion, leg press), 20% 1RM training produced about half the cross-sectional-area gain of 40%, 60% or 80% 1RM. Another cited trial found 70% beat 15% 1RM for biceps thickness.
findings.population: Cited within-subject trials (Lasevicius et al., 12 weeks, volume-load matched; Buckner et al., untrained men and women, 8 weeks)

exercises.name: elbow flexion and leg press at 40–80% 1RM

findings.finding: Cited trials in trained men: volume-load-matched 7×~3RM and 3×~10RM grew biceps similarly, but the heavy group showed joint problems and overtraining signs; 2–6 vs 8–12 reps grew pecs and quads similarly. Set-matched results conflicted (8–12RM beat 2–4RM in one trial, similar in another).
findings.locator: Section 3 (Hypertrophy), heavy- vs moderate-load paragraphs; Section 5
findings.population: Cited trials in resistance-trained men, about 8 weeks

findings.finding: A cited within-subject study (4 sets of standing and seated plantarflexion, twice weekly, 8 weeks) found heavy (6–10RM) and light (20–30RM) loads increased soleus and gastrocnemius thickness similarly.
findings.population: Cited within-subject counterbalanced trial, 8 weeks (participant details not given in the review)

exercises.name: standing and seated plantarflexion (calf raise), heavy 6–10RM
standing and seated plantarflexion (calf raise), light 20–30RM

findings.finding: In untrained men (bench press, 9 weeks), 30–40RM and 100–150RM training raised absolute endurance 39–41% versus 28% for 6–8RM. In untrained women, bench endurance gains favoured 15–20RM (44%) over 6–8RM (31%) and 30–40RM (20%). The review judges load effects equivocal.
findings.population: Cited trials: 43 untrained young men (Anderson and Kearney, 9 weeks); untrained young women (Stone and Coulter)

findings.finding: In untrained women, 30–40RM training raised absolute squat endurance 137%, versus 84% (6–8RM) and 80% (15–20RM), and relative endurance 83% versus 66% and 61%. However, knee extension at 15% vs 70% 1RM gave similar endurance gains.
findings.population: Cited trials: untrained young women (Stone and Coulter); 8-week unilateral knee-extension trial (Jessee et al.)

findings.finding: In a meta-analysis of 21 studies with every set taken to momentary failure for at least 6 weeks, 1RM gains were significantly greater with high loads (>60% 1RM) than low loads (<=60% 1RM). Pooled effect sizes and contributing-study counts were not read.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 28834797). Full text paywalled at journals.lww.com (HTTP 402), not read.
findings.population: 21 studies of participants with no known medical conditions or injuries impairing training; interventions of at least 6 weeks

exercises.name: high-load resistance training (>60% 1RM, sets to failure)
low-load resistance training (<=60% 1RM, sets to failure)

findings.finding: For isometric strength, pooled changes did not differ significantly between high-load (>60% 1RM) and low-load (<=60% 1RM) training to failure. The abstract reports neither an effect size nor how many studies contributed to this outcome.
findings.population: Subset of 21 studies reporting isometric strength (count not given in abstract)

exercises.name: high-load resistance training (>60% 1RM, sets to failure)
low-load resistance training (<=60% 1RM, sets to failure)

findings.finding: In a meta-analysis of 21 studies (all sets to momentary failure, at least 6 weeks), muscle-size changes were similar with low-load (<=60% 1RM) and high-load (>60% 1RM) training. The abstract gives no pooled effect size or contributing-study count.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 28834797). Full text paywalled, not read.
findings.population: 21 studies of participants without conditions impairing training; interventions of at least 6 weeks

exercises.name: high-load resistance training (>60% 1RM, sets to failure)
low-load resistance training (<=60% 1RM, sets to failure)

findings.finding: When both were trained to volitional failure, high loads (<=8RM) gave larger 1RM gains than low loads (>15RM): SMD 0.60 (95% CI 0.38-0.82), P<0.001, 19 comparisons, n=403. Best-quality subgroup: SMD 0.63 (0.38-0.88). These are the original, pre-corrigendum values.
findings.locator: Table 2 (muscle strength, high vs low); Results section 'Resistance training load effects on muscle strength'; Figure 4. Corrigendum (PMID 35029596, PMC12479057) corrected three study effect sizes in Figure 4 (Morton 2016, Jenkins 2017, Ozaki 2018). It says the overall and best-quality pooled effects changed slightly, main conclusions unchanged, and gives no revised pooled numbers in its text.
findings.population: 28 studies, 747 healthy adults (mean age 23.4 y; 21/28 studies untrained, 19/28 men); mean 8.9 weeks

findings.finding: When trained to volitional failure, moderate loads (9-15RM) gave larger 1RM gains than low loads (>15RM): SMD 0.34 (95% CI 0.05-0.62), P=0.003, 9 comparisons, n=152. Best-quality subgroup: SMD 0.35 (0.05-0.65). These are the original, pre-corrigendum values.
findings.locator: Table 2 (muscle strength, moderate vs low); Results section 'Resistance training load effects on muscle strength'. Corrigendum (PMID 35029596) says the overall and best-quality pooled strength effects in Figure 4 changed slightly, conclusions unchanged, with no revised numbers in its text.
findings.population: 28 studies, 747 healthy adults (mostly untrained young men); mean 8.9 weeks

findings.finding: High versus moderate loads to failure: the 1RM advantage for high load was not significant, SMD 0.26 (95% CI -0.02 to 0.54), P=0.068, 10 comparisons, n=125. High load still had a 98.2% probability of ranking best for strength. These are pre-corrigendum values.
findings.locator: Table 2 (muscle strength, high vs moderate; best-intervention probability column); Discussion paragraph on load-dependent strength, which gives P=0.072 for this comparison. Corrigendum (PMID 35029596) says the pooled strength effects changed slightly, conclusions unchanged.
findings.population: 28 studies, 747 healthy adults (mostly untrained young men); mean 8.9 weeks

findings.finding: Hypertrophy did not differ between high (<=8RM) and low (>15RM) loads to failure: SMD 0.12 (95% CI -0.06 to 0.29), P=0.241, 19 comparisons, n=347; hypertrophy-network I2=0%. Best-quality subgroup: SMD 0.10. Training status moderated this comparison (coefficient -1.38, P=0.033).
findings.locator: Table 2 (muscle hypertrophy, high vs low); Table 3 (multivariate meta-regression, training status); Results section 'Resistance training load effects on muscle hypertrophy'
findings.population: 24 hypertrophy studies within 28 studies/747 healthy adults; lower-limb 15, upper-limb 8 and whole-body 5 studies; assessed limb did not moderate results

findings.finding: Moderate (9-15RM) and low (>15RM) loads to failure produced statistically similar hypertrophy: SMD 0.20 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.44), P=0.113, 7 comparisons, n=128. Best-quality subgroup: SMD -0.06 (2 comparisons). More training sessions predicted a larger effect (P=0.031).
findings.locator: Table 2 (muscle hypertrophy, moderate vs low); Table 3 (number of sessions covariate, moderate vs low)
findings.population: Hypertrophy studies within 28 studies/747 healthy adults (mostly untrained young adults)

findings.finding: High (<=8RM) and moderate (9-15RM) loads to failure produced similar hypertrophy: SMD -0.09 (95% CI -0.33 to 0.16), P=0.469, 9 comparisons, n=107. Best-quality subgroup: SMD 0.15. More sessions predicted a larger effect (P=0.045).
findings.locator: Table 2 (muscle hypertrophy, high vs moderate); Table 3 (number of sessions covariate, high vs moderate)
findings.population: Hypertrophy studies within 28 studies/747 healthy adults (mostly untrained young adults)

findings.finding: After 8 weeks of leg press, squat and knee extension, 1RM rose significantly more in the 3-5RM group (4 sets, 3-min rest) than in the 9-11RM or 20-28RM groups. The abstract gives no magnitudes.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 12436270; full text subscription-only at Springer)
findings.population: 32 untrained men (mean age 22.5 y); 3-5RM n=9, 9-11RM n=11, 20-28RM n=7, control n=5; 2 then 3 sessions/week over 8 weeks

exercises.name: 3-5RM x4 sets, 3-min rest (leg press, squat, knee extension)

findings.finding: Maximal repetitions at 60% 1RM improved most in the 20-28RM group (2 sets, 1-min rest) compared with the 3-5RM and 9-11RM groups after 8 weeks of lower-body training. The abstract gives no magnitudes and does not say whether the test used pre- or post-training 1RM.
findings.population: 32 untrained men (mean age 22.5 y); 8 weeks

exercises.name: 20-28RM x2 sets, 1-min rest (leg press, squat, knee extension)

findings.finding: Type I, IIA and IIB fibre cross-sectional areas increased in the 3-5RM and 9-11RM groups but not significantly in the 20-28RM group or controls after 8 weeks. Low and intermediate zones gave similar adaptations. Magnitudes and biopsy site are not stated in the abstract.
findings.population: 32 untrained men (mean age 22.5 y); 8 weeks

exercises.name: 3-5RM x4 sets (leg press, squat, knee extension)

findings.finding: Only the 20-28RM group significantly increased maximal aerobic power and time to exhaustion after 8 weeks of leg press, squat and knee extension. The abstract lists VO2max as measured but does not report its result, and gives no magnitudes.
findings.population: 32 untrained men (mean age 22.5 y); 8 weeks

exercises.name: 20-28RM x2 sets, 1-min rest (leg press, squat, knee extension)

findings.finding: In trained men over 8 weeks, muscle thickness rose similarly with 25-35-rep and 8-12-rep sets to failure (low vs high load): elbow flexors 8.6% vs 5.3%, elbow extensors 5.2% vs 6.0%, quadriceps 9.5% vs 9.3%. No significant group differences.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed 25853914; publisher page full text subscriber-only)
findings.population: 18 resistance-trained young men (n=9 per group); 3 sessions/week for 8 weeks

exercises.name: low-load training, 25-35 reps per set to failure (3 sets x 7 exercises)
high-load training, 8-12 reps per set to failure (3 sets x 7 exercises)

findings.finding: Back squat 1RM improved significantly more with 8-12-rep high-load training than with 25-35-rep low-load training (19.6% vs 8.8%) over 8 weeks in trained men.
findings.population: 18 resistance-trained young men (n=9 per group); 8 weeks

exercises.name: high-load training, 8-12 reps per set to failure
low-load training, 25-35 reps per set to failure

findings.finding: Bench press 1RM showed only a non-significant trend favouring 8-12-rep high-load over 25-35-rep low-load training (6.5% vs 2.0%) after 8 weeks in trained men.
findings.population: 18 resistance-trained young men (n=9 per group); 8 weeks

exercises.name: high-load training, 8-12 reps per set to failure
low-load training, 25-35 reps per set to failure

findings.finding: Bench press repetitions to failure at 50% 1RM improved more with 25-35-rep low-load training than with 8-12-rep high-load training (16.6% vs -1.2%) after 8 weeks. The abstract does not say whether the test load came from pre- or post-training 1RM.
findings.population: 18 resistance-trained young men (n=9 per group); 8 weeks

exercises.name: low-load training, 25-35 reps per set to failure
high-load training, 8-12 reps per set to failure

findings.finding: Across 14 studies, more repetitions per set improved reps-to-failure at a fixed percentage of post-training 1RM more than fewer did: g=0.97 (95% CI 0.53-1.40), P<0.001. High (18-125) vs moderate (7-13) reps: g=1.08 (0.60-1.56). Strength change was a significant meta-regression moderator (P=0.002).
findings.locator: Abstract (publisher page em-consulte.com article 1508096; Western Sydney University research portal). Full text subscription-only (ScienceDirect returned 403), not read.
findings.population: 14 studies (total participants not reported in the abstract)

exercises.name: higher repetitions per set (>=15; subgroup 18-125 reps)

findings.finding: When the endurance test load was set from pre-training 1RM, higher and lower repetitions per set did not differ: g=0.09 (95% CI -0.17 to 0.35), P=0.49. The benefit of high-rep training therefore depends on how the endurance test is loaded.
findings.population: Subset of 14 studies (number of studies and participants in this subset not reported in the abstract)

findings.finding: Untrained men who trained the elbow flexors only with wide-grip lat pulldowns, or only with standing barbell curls (3x8-12RM to failure, twice weekly, 10 weeks), gained similar elbow-flexor thickness: +6.10% vs +5.83%. No between-group difference. Lats were not measured.
findings.locator: Results section; Table 2 (muscle thickness, mm, pre/post); Methods 3.5 (protocol)
findings.population: 29 untrained young men (multi-joint n=14, single-joint n=15); both groups also did leg press, knee flexion and bench press; 10 weeks

findings.finding: Elbow-flexor isokinetic peak torque (60 deg/s) rose similarly after 10 weeks of lat-pulldown-only versus barbell-curl-only training: +10.40% (49.26 to 54.38 Nm) vs +11.87% (49.69 to 55.59 Nm). No between-group difference.
findings.locator: Results section; Table 2 (peak torque, Nm, pre/post)
findings.population: 29 untrained young men (multi-joint n=14, single-joint n=15); 10 weeks

findings.finding: At matched volume load, multi-joint-only training raised bench press 1RM 10.9% versus 8.1% for single-joint-only training; between-group difference significant. Confounds: multi-joint group lifted 6-8RM versus 12-18RM and practised the bench press itself.
findings.population: 36 resistance-training-naive amateur soccer-playing men (group mean ages 23.5 and 25.5 y in Results; Methods text states 28 ± 4.5 y), 3 sessions/week for 8 weeks after 4-week familiarisation

exercises.name: multi-joint-only programme (bench press, incline bench press, military press)
single-joint-only programme (pec deck, incline dumbbell fly, lateral raise)

findings.finding: Squat 1RM rose 13.8% with multi-joint-only training versus 8.3% with single-joint-only training over 8 weeks at matched volume load; between-group difference significant, partly confounded by heavier loads and squat practice in the multi-joint group.
findings.population: 36 resistance-training-naive amateur soccer-playing men (group mean ages 23.5 and 25.5 y in Results; Methods text states 28 ± 4.5 y), 3 sessions/week for 8 weeks after 4-week familiarisation

exercises.name: single-joint-only programme (knee extension, knee flexion, calf raise)

findings.finding: Knee extension 1RM improved more after multi-joint-only training (18.9%) than after the single-joint programme that itself included knee extension (12.4%), at matched volume load; the single-joint group trained with lighter 12-18RM loads.
findings.population: 36 resistance-training-naive amateur soccer-playing men (group mean ages 23.5 and 25.5 y in Results; Methods text states 28 ± 4.5 y), 3 sessions/week for 8 weeks after 4-week familiarisation

exercises.name: single-joint-only programme (knee extension, knee flexion, calf raise)

findings.finding: Cycle-ergometer VO2max rose 12.5% (46.5 to 52.3 ml/kg/min) with multi-joint-only resistance training versus 5.1% with single-joint-only training (between-group p reported as 0.05); all participants were also doing pre-season soccer training.
findings.population: 36 resistance-training-naive amateur soccer-playing men (group mean ages 23.5 and 25.5 y in Results; Methods text states 28 ± 4.5 y), 3 sessions/week for 8 weeks after 4-week familiarisation

findings.finding: Whole-body DXA fat-free mass rose 5.5% (multi-joint) versus 3.5% (single-joint), not significantly different (p=0.08); fat-mass loss was also similar (p=0.09). Fat-free mass is a whole-body proxy, not muscle-specific hypertrophy.
findings.locator: Table 2 (fat-free mass row; Results text states 4.9% for multi-joint)
findings.population: 36 resistance-training-naive amateur soccer-playing men (group mean ages 23.5 and 25.5 y in Results; Methods text states 28 ± 4.5 y), 3 sessions/week for 8 weeks after 4-week familiarisation

findings.finding: Across 43 studies (1,660 participants, 72 interventions, mostly lower body), dynamic training improved the trained lift by SMD 0.98 (95% CI 0.91-1.06) but untrained isometric strength of the same muscles by only SMD 0.42 (0.35-0.49): strength is largely lift-specific.
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 16-60, untrained to resistance-trained; 65 of 72 interventions lower body; interventions of at least 10 sessions

exercises.name: trained dynamic lift (e.g. squat, leg press, knee extension 1RM)
non-trained isometric strength test of the same muscles

findings.finding: Single-joint training (24-25 interventions) transferred more to untrained isometric strength than multi-joint training (44), SMD 0.70 (95% CI 0.53-0.87) versus 0.33; trained-lift gains 1.30 versus 1.02. No subgroup-difference test; position-matched gap smaller (0.47 versus 0.34). Indirect, between-study comparison.
findings.locator: Discussion (single- vs multi-joint and position-matched paragraphs); Results - Study Characteristics; Fig. 4b
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 16-60, mostly lower-body interventions

findings.finding: Meta-regression found that training-induced hypertrophy (13 studies, ultrasound or MRI) and EMG activity changes (9 studies) did not significantly predict gains in dynamic or isometric strength (p>=0.222; 0-13.4% of variance explained).
findings.population: Healthy adults aged 16-60, subset of included studies reporting hypertrophy or EMG

findings.finding: Pooling 7 RCTs (627 people with forward head posture), therapeutic exercise versus control improved craniovertebral angle (pooled odds ratio 6.7, 95% CI 2.53-17.9, p=0.0005). The specific exercises and muscles targeted could not be verified (abstract only).
findings.population: 627 people with forward head posture across 7 RCTs

findings.finding: In the same pooled trials, therapeutic exercise had no significant effect on cranial angle (pooled odds ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.43-1.2, p=0.2) in people with forward head posture; only the abstract could be read.
findings.population: People with forward head posture across the included RCTs (per-analysis n not in abstract)

findings.finding: Across 22 studies (903 people with upper crossed syndrome), therapeutic exercise versus no exercise improved forward head angle (SMD -1.51, 95% CI -1.86 to -1.16; p reported 0.001); heterogeneity high (I2=80%), publication bias detected, 15 of 22 studies non-randomised.
findings.locator: Results - Forward head posture; Fig. 2 (pooled row)
findings.population: 903 people with upper crossed syndrome (children to adults), programmes of at least 3 weeks

exercises.name: therapeutic exercise (strengthening, stretching, scapular stabilisation or combined corrective programme)

findings.finding: In 20 studies (774 participants), therapeutic exercise versus no exercise improved rounded-shoulder angle (SMD -1.49, 95% CI -1.82 to -1.16; p reported 0.001); I2=75%, publication bias detected, and most included studies were non-randomised.
findings.population: 774 people with upper crossed syndrome (children to adults)

exercises.name: therapeutic exercise (strengthening, stretching, scapular stabilisation or combined corrective programme)

findings.finding: In 18 studies (673 participants), therapeutic exercise versus no exercise reduced thoracic kyphosis angle (SMD -1.47, 95% CI -1.84 to -1.10; p reported 0.001); I2=78%, publication bias present. Exercise types were not compared against each other quantitatively.
findings.population: 673 people with upper crossed syndrome (children to adults)

exercises.name: therapeutic exercise (strengthening, stretching, scapular stabilisation or combined corrective programme)

findings.finding: Chronic stretching of hamstrings or hip flexors did not change pelvic tilt or lumbar lordosis versus control (ES -0.04, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.09, p=0.43; 5 studies, 7 effect sizes); acute hamstring stretching was also null (2 studies).
findings.locator: Table 3; Results - Quantitative Synthesis, Stretching; Fig. 2
findings.population: Healthy adults (969 across 23 trials overall); lumbopelvic stretching subgroup

findings.finding: Chronic stretching, mostly of pectoralis minor or major, did not significantly improve thoracic or cervical posture (scapular position, forward shoulder, forward head, thoracic curve) versus control (ES -0.44, 95% CI -1.03 to 0.16, p=0.10; 4 studies, 8 effect sizes).
findings.locator: Table 3; Results - Quantitative Synthesis, Stretching; Fig. 2
findings.population: Healthy adults; thoracic/cervical stretching subgroup

findings.finding: Chronic strengthening (back-extensor, trapezius/rhomboid, scapular-stabiliser and spine-strengthening programmes) improved thoracic/cervical posture versus control: ES -1.04, 95% CI -1.69 to -0.40, p=0.005; 10 studies, 14 effect sizes; trials mostly fair quality. Overall strengthening ES -0.87 (95% CI -1.58 to -0.17).
findings.locator: Table 3; Results - Chronic Strengthening; Fig. 3 (abstract gives overall d=-0.83, p=0.01)
findings.population: Adults without specific pathology, including older adults with hyperkyphosis, women aged 49-65 and two neck-pain trials; thoracic/cervical strengthening subgroup

exercises.name: strengthening (back extensors, trapezius/rhomboids, scapular stabilisers, spine-strengthening programmes)

findings.finding: Back-extensor strengthening did not change lumbopelvic posture (lordosis, sacral and spinal inclination) versus control: ES -0.23, 95% CI -1.45 to 0.98, p=0.25; only 2 studies and 5 effect sizes, so this region is under-researched.
findings.locator: Results - Chronic Strengthening; Table 3 (CI -1.5 to 0.98); Fig. 3 (lumbopelvic rows of Fukuda et al. and Itoi & Sinaki)
findings.population: Middle-aged and older adults (community-dwelling older adults; women aged 49-65); lumbopelvic strengthening subgroup

findings.finding: In head-to-head trials, strengthening beat stretching for posture: d=0.81, 95% CI 0.40-1.22, p=0.004; 6 studies and 9 effect sizes, nearly all targeting the thoracic/cervical region.
findings.population: Six direct stretching-versus-strengthening trials; per Table 1, three appear to enrol people with neck or non-specific back pain

exercises.name: strengthening (e.g. reverse fly, trapezius/rhomboid, shoulder-muscle training)

findings.finding: In younger people with thoracic hyperkyphosis, structured exercise programmes lasting three months or less reduced kyphosis versus control (SMD -2.8, 95% CI -4.3 to -1.3; low-to-moderate quality). Exercise content could not be verified because only the abstract was accessible.
findings.population: Younger adults with thoracic hyperkyphosis (RCTs; per-analysis n not in abstract)

exercises.name: structured exercise programme (3 months or less)

findings.finding: In older adults, exercise programmes of three months or less gave only a small, borderline kyphosis reduction (SMD -0.3, 95% CI -0.6 to 0.0); programmes over three months were judged ineffective, while bracing for three months or more showed SMD -1.0 (low quality).
findings.population: Older adults with thoracic hyperkyphosis (RCTs; per-analysis n not in abstract)

exercises.name: structured exercise programme (3 months or less)

findings.finding: Seven RCTs (10 comparisons, two trials entered twice by measurement method; 457 participants, mostly hyperkyphotic women): supervised exercise reduced thoracic kyphosis versus controls, SMD -1.40 (95% CI -2.15 to -0.66), p=0.0002, high heterogeneity. A higher-quality-only sensitivity analysis was non-significant: SMD -0.49 (-1.18 to 0.20).
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Thoracic kyphosis angle' and Fig 2; Table 1
findings.population: 7 RCTs in adults aged 18-88 y (the adolescent trial measured lordosis only), mostly women; 6 of 7 required kyphosis above 40-45 degrees; programmes 5-30 weeks, 2-3 sessions/week

exercises.name: supervised exercise programmes containing strengthening and/or stretching (back-muscle stretching and strengthening, thoracic correction with elastic band, Pilates, multimodal spinal-extensor strengthening, corrective exercise, hamstring stretching)
supervised exercise programmes containing strengthening and/or stretching

findings.finding: Four RCTs (159 participants): the pooled reduction in lumbar lordosis with exercise versus controls was medium-sized but not statistically significant, SMD -0.53, p=0.40 (the printed CI of -1.76 to -0.70 conflicts with that p-value). The two trials that improved lordosis combined stretching with strengthening.
findings.locator: Abstract; Results, 'Lumbar lordotic angle' and Fig 4; Discussion
findings.population: 4 RCTs: hyperlordotic adolescent girls, adults with low back pain, standing female workers; 2-12 weeks

exercises.name: exercise programmes (hamstring stretching; mat or sling strengthening; Williams stretch-and-strength training; stretching plus aerobic plus strengthening)

findings.finding: Only one of seven kyphosis trials used stretching alone (hamstring stretching, 12 weeks); kyphosis did not change, while the six strengthening-containing programmes improved it. That trial alone did not recruit hyperkyphotic participants. The authors' inference that strengthening matters more is indirect.
findings.locator: Results, 'Thoracic kyphosis angle' and 'Characteristics of the included studies'; Discussion (paragraph on stretching versus strengthening); Table 1 (Muyor et al. 2012)
findings.population: Between-trial comparison within 7 kyphosis RCTs; stretching-only trial in 35-50-year-old women working in a standing position, not selected for hyperkyphosis

findings.finding: Twenty trials. Of 8 using 3-D kinematics, 5 found exercise altered scapular motion (3 in impingement patients). Of 12 using 2-D methods, 8 reported improvements of questionable quality. The authors rate the evidence conflicting, with no clear benefit for scapular position or motion.
findings.locator: Abstract (Results and Conclusion); full text not accessible
findings.population: Adults with scapular dyskinesis, including subacromial impingement patients and asymptomatic individuals; 20 clinical trials

exercises.name: scapular muscle strengthening, stretching and scapular stabilisation exercise

findings.finding: One RCT (30 girls aged 17, 8 weeks): deep neck flexor training improved head tilt, neck flexion and forward shoulder angles on X-ray. The basic neck/shoulder stretching comparison group showed no change.
findings.population: 30 female high-school students with neck pain for 3 months or more, 8 weeks

findings.finding: One RCT (58 women, 6 weeks): deep neck flexor training reduced forward-head drift during a 10-minute computer task compared with cervical flexor endurance-strength training. Both groups improved upper-thoracic posture, with no difference between groups.
findings.population: 58 women with chronic neck pain, 6 weeks

findings.finding: Meta-analysis of 3 RCTs: cervical flexor strength-endurance training showed a non-significant trend toward more neck flexor strength than deep flexor training (p=0.10). In one RCT (58 women), endurance-strength training significantly increased flexor strength; deep flexor training did not.
findings.locator: Results, 'Kinetics - Strength' and Fig 4; Table 1 (Falla 2006, O'Leary 2007, O'Leary 2012)
findings.population: 3 RCTs in adults with chronic neck pain (mostly women), 6-10 weeks

exercises.name: cervical flexor strength-endurance training (including head-lift exercise)

findings.finding: Meta-analysis of 3 RCTs: no significant difference in craniocervical flexor endurance between deep neck flexor training and strength-endurance regimes, with large between-study variation. In one trial, craniocervical endurance training at 20% MVC lengthened time-to-failure significantly more than deep flexor training at 10 weeks.
findings.locator: Results, 'Kinetics - Endurance' and Fig 5; Table 1 (Ghaderi 2017, O'Leary 2007, O'Leary 2012)
findings.population: 3 RCTs in adults with chronic neck pain (mostly women), 6-10 weeks

exercises.name: cervical flexor strength-endurance or endurance training (20% MVC craniocervical flexor endurance, head-lift, isometric resistance)

findings.finding: Meta-analysis of 3 RCTs (106 participants): after deep neck flexor training, sternocleidomastoid EMG during the craniocervical flexion test was lower than after strength-endurance training or no exercise, at all five stages. This is a coordination change, not evidence of strength.
findings.locator: Results, 'Neuromuscular function - CCFT EMG amplitude' and Fig 3; Table 1 (Jull 2009, Ghaderi 2017, Beer 2012)
findings.population: 3 RCTs in adults with chronic neck pain, 2-10 weeks

findings.finding: One RCT (60 adults, 10 weeks): deep neck flexor training increased longus colli cross-sectional area, width and thickness on ultrasound compared with cervical flexor strength training. It did not change sternocleidomastoid thickness.
findings.population: 60 adults (40 women, 20 men) with chronic neck pain, 10 weeks

findings.finding: Same RCT (60 adults, 10 weeks): cervical flexor strength training significantly increased superficial sternocleidomastoid thickness compared with deep neck flexor training. It did not change longus colli dimensions.
findings.population: 60 adults (40 women, 20 men) with chronic neck pain, 10 weeks

findings.finding: Network meta-analysis of 4 RCTs: neither resistance training (SMD 0.18, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.64) nor stabilisation/motor control (0.21, -0.28 to 0.69) significantly increased trunk muscle strength versus no intervention. Pairwise, all exercise versus control gave SMD 0.29 (0.00 to 0.58), p=0.050. GRADE low.
findings.locator: Results, 'Muscle strength'; Table 2 (muscle strength rows); Table 3
findings.population: Adults with non-specific chronic low back pain; 4 RCTs in the strength network (6 in pairwise)

findings.finding: Pairwise meta-analysis of 5 RCTs covering seven exercise types: exercise improved objectively measured trunk muscle endurance versus no intervention, SMD 1.57 (95% CI 0.69 to 2.45), p<0.001, I2=87%. The review could not compare exercise modes against each other for endurance.
findings.population: Adults with non-specific chronic low back pain; 5 RCTs

exercises.name: exercise training (aerobic, McKenzie, Pilates, resistance, stretching, water-based, other)

findings.finding: Meta-analysis of 4 RCTs (172 participants): isolated lumbar extension machine training with the pelvis stabilised gave a non-significant gain in isometric lumbar extension strength versus no-exercise controls. Hedges g 0.967 (95% CI -0.35 to 2.28), p=0.150, I2=93%; GRADE very low.
findings.population: Adults (mean about 41.5 y) with chronic non-specific low back pain; 8-12 weeks, 1-2 sessions/week, mostly MedX machine

exercises.name: isolated lumbar extension machine training with pelvic stabilisation

findings.finding: One RCT (Smith et al., 42 participants in total): lumbar extension with the pelvis stabilised gave significantly more lumbar extension strength than without stabilisation, at 0-27 degrees. The authors reason that an unrestrained pelvis lets the glutes and hamstrings take over the lift.
findings.locator: Discussion, 'Effects of ILEX on physical functionality related outcomes' and pain section; Table 2
findings.population: Adults with chronic low back pain (6 months or more), 12 weeks, one set to fatigue weekly

exercises.name: lumbar extension with pelvic stabilisation (isolated lumbar extension)

findings.finding: One RCT (107 men, 10 weeks): isolated lumbar extension machine training raised lumbar extensor isometric torque by 14.0%, against 16.5% after regular physiotherapy training. The review reports the strength gains as comparable.
findings.locator: Table 5 (Helmhout et al.); Discussion, 'Effects of ILEX on physical functionality related outcomes'
findings.population: 107 men with low back pain for 4 weeks or more, 10 weeks

findings.finding: One RCT (Bruce-Low et al., 12 weeks, 8-12 reps at about 80% of maximum torque): one weekly session of isolated lumbar extension produced strength gains similar to two weekly sessions. The review gives no between-frequency statistics.
findings.locator: Discussion, 'Effects of ILEX on physical functionality related outcomes'; Table 3
findings.population: Adults with chronic low back pain (6 months or more), 12 weeks

findings.finding: One RCT (Fortin et al., 50 adults, 12 weeks), cited by the review, reported larger erector spinae and multifidus cross-sectional area after isolated lumbar extension. The review gives no between-group result against the general resistance-exercise control, so superiority is unknown.
findings.locator: Discussion, 'Effects of ILEX on pain-related outcomes'; Table 2; Table 3
findings.population: 50 adults with chronic low back pain (3 months or more), 12 weeks, 2 sessions/week

findings.finding: In 8 studies (118 circuit trainees) VO2max rose pre-post (SMD 1.10, 95% CI 0.81–1.39; I² 72%; mean gain about 9.7%). In the 6 studies with non-training controls, circuit training outperformed controls (SMD 0.83, 0.52–1.14; I² 65%).
findings.locator: Results 3.1; Fig. 2a-b; Table 1; Discussion 4 (UCAM repository copy of the article)
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y, mostly active men; 6-20 week circuit programmes

findings.finding: In 8 studies (237 circuit trainees) bench press 1RM rose pre-post (SMD 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.77; I² 76%; mean gain about 13.2%). In the 6 studies with controls, circuit training outperformed controls (SMD 0.94, 0.64–1.24; I² 81%).
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y (sedentary, active and trained); 5-14 week circuit programmes

findings.finding: Subgroup contrasts: VO2max gains were larger with circuits at ≥60% 1RM than <60% (ES 2.08 vs 0.90, p=0.004), programmes ≤12 weeks vs longer (2.34 vs 0.71, p=0.005) and sessions <30 min (1.85 vs 0.71, p=0.03).
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y; 8 VO2max studies

exercises.name: resistance circuit training at 60% 1RM or more

findings.finding: Bench 1RM gains were larger with circuits at <60% 1RM than ≥60% (ES 1.75 vs 0.56, p=0.001) and sessions <60 min (1.27 vs 0.41, p=0.01); sedentary subjects gained most (1.92). Authors attribute the light-load advantage partly to lower baseline fitness.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y; 8 bench press studies

exercises.name: resistance circuit training at 60% 1RM or more

findings.finding: Circuit arms improved VO2max by MD 2.93 mL/kg/min (95% CI 1.97–3.90; 28 groups, n=367; I² 76%), about 6.3%, while controls did not change (0.03); between-group difference significant (Z=7.53, p<0.001). Aerobic performance SMD 0.65 vs −0.11.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y (reported 18-42.5 y); mean 10 weeks (4-28), 2-3 sessions/week

findings.finding: Whole-body muscle (lean/fat-free) mass rose in circuit arms (SMD 0.28, 95% CI 0.07–0.49; 14 groups, n=181) but not controls (−0.05); text reports +1.18 kg (~1.9%). Only untrained participants gained significantly (SMD 0.30).
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y; whole-body lean mass proxy, not muscle-specific

findings.finding: Bench press 1RM rose in circuit arms (SMD 1.16, 95% CI 0.84–1.47; 27 groups, n=404; I² 75%) versus no change in controls (0.11, −0.09 to 0.31); authors flag funnel-plot asymmetry for strength outcomes.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y; circuit programmes 4-28 weeks

findings.finding: Front pull-down 1RM rose by MD 11.61 kg (95% CI 8.83–14.39; 5 groups, n=61) with circuit training versus −0.30 kg (−3.21 to 2.60) in controls; the between-group difference was reported significant.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y

findings.finding: Elbow-flexion 1RM rose by MD 5.00 kg (95% CI 3.09–6.92; 9 groups, n=121; I² 87%) with circuit training versus −0.41 kg (−1.44 to 0.62) in controls; the between-group difference was reported significant.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y

findings.finding: Handgrip rose marginally in circuit arms (MD 2.15, 95% CI 0.01–4.28, p=0.05; 6 groups, n=95) and non-significantly in controls (1.40, −1.46 to 4.25); no significant between-group difference was reported for handgrip.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y

findings.finding: Circuit arms improved leg press 1RM (SMD 1.83, 95% CI 1.15–2.52; n=177) and half-squat 1RM (SMD 1.20, 0.72–1.67; n=190); controls did not change (0.25 and 0.02); between-group differences significant; strength funnel plots asymmetric.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y; leg press 9 circuit groups, half-squat 11 circuit groups

findings.finding: Leg extension 1RM rose in circuit arms (SMD 1.28, 95% CI 0.83–1.74; 17 groups, n=201; I² 74%) versus 0.08 (−0.17 to 0.33) in controls; the between-group difference was reported significant.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y

findings.finding: Countermovement jump height rose in circuit arms (MD 3.58, 95% CI 2.69–4.47; 11 groups, n=118; I² 22%) versus 0.43 (−0.16 to 1.01) in controls; CMJ was the only strength-type outcome without funnel-plot asymmetry.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y

findings.finding: VO2max improved in men, women, trained, active and untrained groups; no significant subgroup differences by intensity, sets, repetitions, rest or session count, though effects trended larger with 3 days/week and more than 20 sessions.
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y

findings.finding: Leg press gains were larger with 3 vs 2 sessions/week (SMD 1.53; χ²=14.12, p<0.001), 21–30 sessions (SMD 1.83; χ²=15.18, p<0.001) and in untrained adults (SMD 1.74). Bench press subgroup reporting is internally inconsistent (Results χ²=20.11, p<0.001; Discussion: no differences).
findings.population: Healthy adults 18-65 y

findings.finding: HIFT beat no-exercise controls for endurance capacity (SMD 0.42, 95% CI 0.07–0.78; 8 studies, 18 effect sizes). Tests were VO2max, walk/run distance or time, Bruce/Cunningham treadmill tests and one skipping test. Females responded more than mixed samples (p=0.02).
findings.locator: Results: HIFT vs. no exercise; Fig. 2 (forest plot); Table 3 (moderators)
findings.population: Review total 864 healthy participants (mean ages 11.7-72.8 y); endurance-vs-NEX subset of 8 studies, HIFT 4-18 weeks

findings.finding: HIFT and moderate continuous endurance training produced similar endurance gains (SMD −0.11, 95% CI −1.17 to 0.95; 4 studies, 9 effect sizes); the wide interval does not establish equivalence and moderators could not be tested.
findings.locator: Results: HIFT vs. endurance training; Fig. 5
findings.population: Healthy mostly young adults; HIFT 4-16 weeks

exercises.name: moderate continuous endurance training (running or walking)

findings.finding: HIFT and conventional running or rowing HIIT produced similar endurance gains (SMD −0.15, 95% CI −1.4 to 1.1; 3 studies, 5 effect sizes); too few studies for moderator or publication-bias analysis.
findings.locator: Results: HIFT vs. endurance training; Fig. 6
findings.population: Healthy recreationally active or moderately trained young adults; 4-16 weeks

findings.finding: HIFT improved pooled strength versus no exercise (SMD 0.60, 95% CI 0.02–1.18; 7 studies, 44 effect sizes). Pooled tests mixed machine strength tests, push-up/sit-up/plank/burpee repetition tests, handgrip, arm curl and sit-to-stand; no jump tests. No trials compared HIFT with resistance training.
findings.locator: Results: HIFT vs. no exercise; Fig. 3 (forest plot)
findings.population: Review total 864 healthy participants (mean ages 11.7-72.8 y); strength-vs-NEX subset of 7 studies, HIFT 4-18 weeks

findings.finding: HIFT improved strength versus controls (Hedges g 1.380, 95% CI 0.770–1.990; 14 RCTs, n=659; I² 43%); authors rate GRADE low. Participants were 10–23 years, mainly athletes and cadets; strength tests were not tabulated.
findings.population: Healthy individuals aged 10-23 y, mostly athletes, cadets and students; 5 weeks to 3 years

findings.finding: HIFT improved power (g 1.320, 95% CI 0.537–2.103; 13 RCTs, n=476; I² 61%) and speed (g 3.093, 1.432–4.754; n=186) versus controls; GRADE low for both; test protocols were not tabulated.
findings.locator: Results: power and speed; Fig. 4B and 5A; Table 2 (GRADE)
findings.population: Healthy individuals aged 10-23 y, mostly athletes, cadets and students

findings.finding: HIFT improved agility versus controls (g 2.086, 95% CI 1.112–3.060; I² 62%); the GRADE table lists 9 RCTs and 319 participants while the text says seven studies; GRADE low.
findings.population: Healthy individuals aged 10-23 y, mostly athletes, cadets and students

findings.finding: Concurrent resistance-plus-aerobic training and resistance-only training produced no significant difference in upper-limb 1RM (SMD 0.12, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.41; p=0.43). The abstract gives neither exercises tested nor per-outcome study counts.
findings.locator: Abstract (PubMed); full text closed access, not read
findings.population: 21 RCTs, 796 healthy adults

findings.finding: Lower-limb 1RM did not differ significantly between concurrent and resistance-only training (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.79 to 0.15; p=0.19); the point estimate leans toward resistance-only and the interval includes a moderate deficit.
findings.population: 21 RCTs, 796 healthy adults

findings.finding: Concurrent training did not significantly differ from aerobic-only training for aerobic capacity: VO2max SMD −0.19 (95% CI −0.71 to 0.33; p=0.48) and VO2peak SMD −0.24 (−0.57 to 0.08; p=0.14).
findings.population: 21 RCTs, 796 healthy adults

findings.finding: In adults over 60, resistance training of 24 weeks or less raised VO2peak (MD 1.89 mL/kg/min, 95% CI 1.21–2.57; I² 77%), 6MWT distance (MD 30.89, 26.7–35.08; 12 studies) and threshold AT (MD 1.27 mL/kg/min, 0.44–2.09; 4 studies).
findings.locator: Results: VO2peak, six-minute walk test, aerobic threshold; Figs 2-4
findings.population: 37 RCTs, 1641 healthy adults over 60 (832 resistance, 809 control; mean age about 70)

findings.finding: Resistance programmes longer than 24 weeks showed no VO2peak change versus controls (MD −0.01 mL/kg/min, 95% CI −1.19 to 1.17; 3 studies, I² 0%) and no significant 6MWT change (MD 19.9, −28.34 to 68.14; 1 study).
findings.locator: Results: VO2peak and six-minute walk test; Figs 2-3; Discussion
findings.population: Healthy adults over 60; long-duration subset only

exercises.name: resistance exercise training longer than 24 weeks

findings.finding: Across pooled trials, combining resistance and endurance training produced VO2max changes not significantly different from endurance training alone (SMD -0.12, 95% CI -0.28 to 0.05). Citrate synthase activity, state 3 respiration, protein synthesis rate and PGC-1alpha mRNA likewise showed no between-group differences.
findings.locator: Abstract (results sentences on overall VO2max and mitochondrial markers)
findings.population: Pooled trials including untrained and athletic populations; number of studies and total participants not reported in the abstract

findings.finding: Where the concurrent program used a reduced endurance-training load, VO2max improved less than with endurance training alone in untrained people (SMD -0.32, 95% CI -0.62 to -0.02) and in 16-week interventions (SMD -0.63, 95% CI -1.21 to -0.06). Athletes showed no significant difference.
findings.locator: Abstract (subgroup results for untrained individuals and 16-week training)
findings.population: Subgroups of untrained individuals and of 16-week interventions; number of studies per subgroup not reported in the abstract

exercises.name: concurrent training with reduced endurance-training load

findings.finding: Preacher and incline curls to failure at 70% of biceps-curl 1RM (n=36) showed no significant between-exercise difference in MVIC-referenced peak or integrated sEMG of the last 3 reps for any region; the abstract does not name the muscle. Authors conclude sEMG cannot predict regional hypertrophy.
findings.population: 36 participants; sex, training status, recorded muscle and electrode regions not stated in the abstract; single acute session

findings.finding: Of 14 included studies, 13 found anatomical cross-sectional area increased more in some muscle regions than others; which region gained most varied (distal, middle, or unreported). Authors conclude growth is uneven in quadriceps femoris, triceps brachii and biceps brachii.
findings.population: 14 included studies; participant numbers and training protocols not reported in the abstract

exercises.name: regions within one muscle after resistance training (proximal vs middle vs distal); the abstract does not compare exercises
